linkedin.title: The Credit Gap: Only 42% of Small Businesses Get the Loan They Asked For
linkedin.subtitle: The Federal Reserve's 2026 data shows most founders are funding growth with partial approvals and personal guarantees. Here's how to plan for the money you'll actually get.
linkedin.html:
Every founder who has applied for a business loan knows the moment. The application is in, the plan is built around the number, and then the answer comes back: yes, but not all of it.

According to the Federal Reserve's 2026 Report on Employer Firms, that "yes, but" is now the most common experience in small business lending. In other words, the plan you build around the loan is usually not the plan you get to execute. This article breaks down what the data says, why it matters more than most founders admit, and how to run your business so a partial approval doesn't break it.

What the Federal Reserve found

The survey covered 6,525 small businesses with 1 to 499 employees. 60% applied for financing in the prior year. Yet of the firms that applied, only 42% received the full amount they sought. Another 36% received some or most of it, and 22% received nothing at all.

Put simply, more than half of applicants walked away without the full amount they needed. That's not an edge case. It's the norm.

Consider what usually happens next. You asked for $250,000 to cover inventory, two hires and a system upgrade. Instead, you get $140,000. Now every leader on your team needs an answer to the same question: which part of the plan dies?

The number founders rarely talk about

Meanwhile, there is a second number founders rarely discuss in public. Among firms with outstanding debt, 59% used a personal guarantee, and 51% pledged business assets.

In practice, that means the majority of small business borrowing is tied directly to the founder's house, savings and family security. Consequently, the stress of a loan decision is never just financial; it's personal. Founders lie awake not because the spreadsheet is complicated, but because the downside lands at their kitchen table.

Why so many founders are borrowing now

The pressure behind those applications is not reckless expansion. Instead, it is cost. 77% of employer firms named rising costs or tariff-related costs as a financial challenge in the Fed survey. Tariff costs hit retail (69%) and manufacturing (62%) hardest.

At the same time, NFIB's October 2026 data shows credit is getting more expensive and less routine. Only 25% of owners borrow regularly, compared with a historical average of 34%, and a net 13% reported paying a higher interest rate on their most recent loan. As a result, the founders who do borrow are often borrowing under pressure, at worse terms, and for survival as much as growth.

Where the full approvals actually happen

Fortunately, the data also points to a better path. Small banks fully approved 57% of applicants, the highest full-approval rate of any lender type in the survey.

That matters, because many founders go straight to the biggest bank they already use or to an online lender with a fast form. Speed feels like progress. However, the data suggests that relationships, local knowledge and a banker who understands your business still win more complete approvals.

Five ways to plan for a partial "yes"

The smartest founders don't hope for the full amount. Rather, they plan for the realistic one. Here's how.

1. Build three versions of the plan. Before you apply, write the plan at 100%, 60% and 0% of the requested amount. Decide in advance what gets cut at each level. Therefore, when the answer comes, you execute instead of panic.

2. Rank every use of funds by payback. Inventory that sells in 60 days pays back faster than a new office. A sales hire with a clear pipeline pays back faster than a brand refresh. Fund the fastest payback first.

3. Start the small-bank relationship before you need it. Open an account, meet the commercial lender, share your numbers quarterly. Then, when you apply, you're a known business, not a file.

4. Negotiate the guarantee, not just the rate. Founders fixate on interest rates. Yet limiting a personal guarantee, capping it, or setting conditions for its release can matter far more to your family's risk. Ask; many founders never do.

5. Fix the cash flow before you borrow for it. If late-paying customers are the reason you need a line of credit, a deposit policy or shorter terms may solve part of the problem for free. Borrowing to finance other people's slow payments is expensive.

What lenders look at before they say "some of it"

A partial approval is rarely random. Instead, it usually reflects specific concerns a lender has about your business. Knowing them in advance lets you fix them, or at least address them in your application.

  • Cash-flow coverage. Can current operating cash flow cover the new payment with room to spare? If the answer depends on growth that hasn't happened yet, expect a smaller number.
  • Customer concentration. If one or two customers drive most of your revenue, the lender sees a single point of failure.
  • Clean, current books. Late or messy financials signal risk, even when the business is healthy. Up-to-date statements are the cheapest credibility you can buy.
  • A clear use of funds. "Working capital" is vague. "Inventory for the Q2 contract with these three customers" is specific, measurable and easier to approve.
  • Owner reliance. If the business can't run without you, the lender is lending to you personally, which is exactly why guarantees appear.

Each of these is fixable. Moreover, each one makes the business stronger whether or not you borrow.

A scenario worth rehearsing

Imagine a services firm doing $1.8M a year. The founder applies for $300,000 to hire three people for a new contract. The bank approves $180,000 with a personal guarantee.

Without a plan, the founder takes the money, hires all three anyway and hopes the contract pays fast. With a plan, the founder hires two, negotiates a 30% deposit from the client to fund the third, and asks the bank to release the guarantee after twelve months of on-time payments. Same approval, very different risk. The difference isn't the loan; it's the thinking before signing.

The decision nobody should make alone

Here's what the data doesn't show: how many of these decisions are made by one person, late at night, without a second opinion.

Should you sign the guarantee? Should you take the partial loan or walk away? Should you cut the hire or the inventory? These are exactly the decisions where an experienced outside perspective is worth the most, and exactly where most founders have the least of it. Bankers are paid to lend. Brokers are paid to place. Your team depends on you to look certain.

That's the gap The Lonely Entrepreneur was built to fill.

medium.title: The 11 P.M. Problem: Founder Loneliness Is a Business Risk, Not a Feelings Problem
medium.subtitle: 55% of business owners wish they had someone to turn to. Here's what isolation does to your decisions, and how the best founders fix it.
medium.html:
It's 11 p.m. The kids are asleep, the team went home hours ago, and you're still at the kitchen table with the same question you've been carrying all week. Should you let your operations manager go? Should you take the bigger client with the brutal payment terms? Should you raise prices or wait one more quarter?

Nobody is going to answer it for you. That's the job. But here's the part founders rarely say out loud: for most of them, nobody is even going to hear it.

That isolation is usually treated as a mood, something to manage with a run, a vacation or a podcast. However, the data, and the experience of thousands of founders, suggests something more serious. Loneliness is a business risk. It shapes the quality of the decisions your company lives or dies by.

What the numbers say about the founder's inner life

A YouGov survey for the Start Up Loans Company, part of the British Business Bank, asked small business owners what running a business actually feels like. The answers were remarkably consistent.

64% feel the constant mental load of being responsible for the business's success. 55% wish they had someone to turn to for support. 51% struggle with work-life balance, and 44% have felt lonely or isolated while running their company. Yet only 38% actively connect with other business leaders.

In other words, most founders want a sounding board, and most don't have one.

The founders who feel it most

The same research shows that isolation isn't evenly spread. It hits hardest exactly where the stakes feel highest.

65% of owners in their first year report feeling lonely. Among microbusiness owners with fewer than ten employees, 56% have felt isolated, compared with 37% to 38% of leaders at larger firms. That makes sense: the smaller the company, the fewer peers you have inside it. There's no CFO to argue with, no COO to share the load, no board meeting forcing a second opinion.

Interestingly, loneliness dips for owners in the middle years and then rises again for those trading twenty years or more (40%). Experience, it turns out, doesn't cure isolation. It often just makes founders better at hiding it.

How loneliness damages decisions

Why should a business owner treat this as more than a personal struggle? Because decisions made alone tend to fail in three predictable ways.

1. They get delayed. Without anyone to talk it through with, hard decisions sit. A founder knows a key hire isn't working but waits six months. A price increase is "planned for next quarter" for a year. Bluevine's 2026 research found that 68% of owners delayed or avoided a major business decision in the past year because of financial stress. Each month of delay has a cost, even when it doesn't show up on the P&L.

2. They get distorted. Alone, the mind tends to swing between two extremes: catastrophe and denial. Either everything is about to collapse, or everything will be fine if we just push harder. Neither is analysis. A good peer conversation pulls you back to the middle, where the actual facts are.

3. They get hidden. When there's no one to explain your reasoning to, it never gets tested. Assumptions stay unexamined, and the team only sees the outcome, never the logic. As a result, the company can't learn from its founder's decisions, good or bad.

Why "just talk to someone" doesn't work

The standard advice is to talk to your spouse, your friends or a mentor. That advice is well meant, but it often fails for structural reasons.

Your spouse already carries the financial risk with you; every worry you share becomes their worry, too. Friends who haven't run a business tend to offer encouragement rather than analysis ("you'll figure it out"). Your team can't be your confidant, because they need you steady. Advisors and vendors often have a financial interest in a particular answer. And a single mentor, however wise, is one perspective with limited time.

What founders actually need is more specific: people who have faced the same decisions, who will tell them the truth, and who have nothing to sell them.

What the best founders do differently

Founders who handle isolation well don't necessarily have more friends. Rather, they build systems for outside input. Here are the habits that show up again and again.

They name the decision precisely. "I'm stressed about cash" isn't a decision. "Do I cut the marketing contractor or delay my own pay for two months?" is. Writing the actual choice in one sentence is half the battle.

They separate facts from fears. On one side of the page: what they know. On the other: what they're afraid of. Most of the weight usually sits on the fears side.

They get two outside perspectives. Not ten. Two people who have lived something similar, ideally from different industries.

They set a decision date. A hard decision without a deadline becomes a permanent resident in your head. A date turns it into a task.

They meet peers regularly, not only in a crisis. The founders who get the most from peer groups show up when things are fine. That way, the trust is already there when things aren't.

The cost of carrying it alone

It's worth being concrete about what isolation costs. Patriot Software's 2026 survey of 1,000 owners found that 53.5% lose sleep over their business at least a few times a week, and 47.7% have skipped or delayed their own paycheck. Only 22.5% describe their mental health as thriving.

Sleep-deprived, underpaid, isolated decision-makers running companies that employ millions of people. That isn't a wellness story. It's an economic one.

What a good peer conversation sounds like

Not every conversation helps. In fact, venting without structure can make a decision feel heavier. The conversations that move founders forward tend to follow a simple pattern.

First, the founder states the decision and the deadline. Next, peers ask questions before they give opinions: what have you tried, what does the data say, what happens if you do nothing? Then, the people who've faced something similar share what they did and what they'd change. Finally, the founder commits to a next step out loud.

That last part matters more than it sounds. A commitment made in front of people you respect is far more likely to happen than one made silently at midnight. Consequently, the best peer groups don't just lower stress; they raise follow-through.

Where The Lonely Entrepreneur fits

Michael Dermer founded The Lonely Entrepreneur after building a company to 1,000 employees and experiencing firsthand how isolating the founder's seat can be. Today TLE has helped more than 500,000 founders, and its programs are built specifically to replace the 11 p.m. kitchen-table conversation with a better one:

  • The Learning Community gives founders under $1M in revenue unlimited group coaching, weekly live sessions with Michael, 5,000+ learning modules, tools and templates, and Entrepreneur Success Managers. Most of all, it gives you a room of founders who've been where you are.
  • The Founder Clarity Hour is a 60-minute one-on-one with a senior consultant for the one decision you can't stop thinking about. You leave with a written plan and three dos and three don'ts.
  • The Founder Blueprint is a five-week program for $1M to $5M founders that rebuilds the plan across customers, team, money, the CEO role and AI, with five hours of one-on-one coaching.
  • Sidekick pairs $5M to $50M CEOs with a senior partner for weekly check-ins, so the biggest calls always get a second set of eyes.
  • Not sure where to start? The free Dermer Diagnosis scores your business across five areas in about eight minutes and shows you where the biggest exposures are.

A simple exercise for tonight

Before you close the laptop, write down the one decision you've been carrying. One sentence. Then write the name of one person who has made a decision like it. Tomorrow, send them a message.

If you can't think of a name, that's the clearest signal of all. It's time to find your room.

Frequently asked questions

How common is loneliness among business owners? In YouGov research for the Start Up Loans Company, 44% of owners had felt lonely or isolated, rising to 65% in the first year of trading. 55% wish they had someone to turn to.

What helps founders make better decisions alone? Naming the decision precisely, separating facts from fears, getting two outside perspectives from people who've faced it, and setting a decision date.

Who gives founders the most honest advice? Other founders who have faced similar decisions and have nothing to sell, ideally in a structured, regular peer setting.

Where can founders find that kind of peer support? The Lonely Entrepreneur's Learning Community offers unlimited group coaching and weekly live sessions with Michael Dermer, plus a community of founders at similar stages.

  • Patriot Software small business owner burnout survey 2026

substack.subtitle: NFIB's October 2026 data shows record caution. But half of owners are still investing. Here's how to make growth decisions when nothing feels certain.

There's a sentence every founder has said at least once this year: "Let's wait and see."

Wait and see what the economy does. Wait and see where rates land. Wait and see how tariffs shake out, whether the big client renews, whether next quarter looks better. It sounds prudent. Often, it is. However, the latest data suggests that for many owners, waiting has quietly become the strategy itself, and that's where the trap begins.

What NFIB's October 2026 data shows

The National Federation of Independent Business surveys its members every month, and its October 2026 report paints a picture of deep caution.

  • Only 11% of owners say now is a good time to expand.
  • Plans for capital outlays in the next six months fell to 21%, the third straight monthly decline.
  • Yet 52% did make capital outlays in the past six months.

Read those three numbers together and a pattern emerges. Owners say it's a bad time to expand. They plan less investment. And yet half of them keep investing anyway, because the business needs it. Trucks break. Software expires. Competitors move. Customers expect more.

In other words, the decision isn't really "invest or don't." It's "invest deliberately or invest reactively."

Why owners say it's not a good time

When NFIB asks owners who think it's not a good time to expand why, the answers are revealing.

31% cite economic conditions, 7% the political climate, 6% the cost of expansion, and 4% financing and interest rates.

Notice what's at the top: general economic conditions. Not a specific cost. Not a specific customer problem. A broad, external feeling of uncertainty. That matters, because uncertainty is not a plan. It's a mood. And moods are terrible at allocating capital.

The hidden cost of waiting

Waiting feels free. It isn't. Here's what it actually costs.

Competitors who move take the ground you leave. In every downturn and every uncertain stretch, some companies invest in talent, marketing and product while others freeze. When conditions improve, the gap is already there.

Talent doesn't wait. The great hire you passed on in March is working for someone else in June. NFIB's own data shows 36% of owners have openings they can't fill. Good people are scarce; delays make them scarcer.

Deferred maintenance compounds. The system you didn't upgrade, the process you didn't fix, the price you didn't raise. Each one costs a little more every month.

Your team reads your hesitation. When the founder waits on everything, people stop bringing ideas. Momentum is hard to restart once it stalls.

None of this means you should expand recklessly. Rather, it means "wait" should be a decision with a date, not a default.

How the winners move anyway

Founders who keep growing through uncertain periods aren't braver. They simply make different kinds of bets. Here's what that looks like.

1. They make the bet smaller. Instead of opening a second location, they test a pop-up or a partner shelf. Instead of hiring three salespeople, they hire one and measure for ninety days. Small bets let you learn without risking the company.

2. They make the bet reversible. Month-to-month leases, contractors before employees, pilots before full rollouts. If you can undo it, you can afford to try it.

3. They set a stop signal in advance. Before investing, they write down the specific result that would make them stop: "If we don't have five paying customers by June 30, we pause." That way, emotion doesn't decide when to quit.

4. They fund growth from what's working. Rather than borrowing for a new idea, they double down on the product, channel or customer type that's already profitable.

5. They stress-test the plan with people who've done it. A growth plan that only the founder has seen is a hypothesis. A plan that three experienced founders have poked holes in is a strategy.

A simple framework: the 3-scenario expansion test

Before your next growth decision, run this quick test.

Scenario A: things get better. Revenue rises 10%, costs stay flat. Does the investment pay back faster? By how much?

Scenario B: things stay the same. This is the most likely case. Does the investment still pay back within a timeframe you can live with?

Scenario C: things get worse. Revenue drops 15%. Can you survive the investment? Can you reverse it? What do you cut first?

If the bet works in B and survives C, it's probably a good bet regardless of what the headlines say. If it only works in A, you're not investing; you're hoping.

  1. What exactly are we buying? A customer segment, a capability, capacity or a location? Be specific.
  2. What's the payback period in the most likely scenario? If you can't estimate it, you're not ready.
  3. What has to be true for this to work? List the assumptions, then mark which ones you've actually tested.
  4. What's the smallest version we could try first? There almost always is one.
  5. Who on the team owns it? Growth initiatives without an owner become the founder's second job.
  6. What will we stop doing to make room? Every yes needs a no somewhere else, especially in time and attention.
  7. Who outside the company has seen this plan? If the answer is nobody, fix that before you spend.

The NFIB data doesn't break down exactly what owners invest in, but the pattern among resilient small businesses is familiar. They tend to invest in things that make the existing business stronger, rather than in big new bets. That means equipment that raises capacity or cuts labor, software and AI tools that remove repetitive work, training for the people they already have, and marketing aimed at their most profitable customers.

In other words, the smartest investments in uncertain times often look boring. They lower costs, protect margins and build capacity that will matter when demand returns. They rarely make headlines, but they compound.

Here's a hard truth many founders recognize once they hear it said plainly: "wait and see" is often a polite way of saying "I don't know how to decide this, and I don't have anyone to decide it with."

That's not a character flaw. It's a structural problem. Big growth decisions involve money, people, risk and timing all at once. Most founders make them alone, with partial data, while running the business day to day. Waiting feels safer than being wrong in front of everyone.

The fix isn't more confidence. It's better input.

Not sure which area of the business is holding growth back? The free Dermer Diagnosis scores five areas in about eight minutes and ranks your biggest exposures.

beehiiv.title: Prices Up, Profits Down: Inside the 2026 Price-Profit Squeeze
beehiiv.subtitle: A net 33% of owners raised prices, yet net earnings sit at -23%. Here's why price increases aren't saving margins, and how to price your way out properly.
beehiiv.html:
If you raised your prices this year and still feel like you're making less money, you're not imagining it. You're also not alone.

NFIB's October 2026 survey shows small business owners raising prices at more than twice the historical rate, and planning even more increases. Yet profits keep falling. That's the price-profit squeeze, and it's one of the most dangerous traps a growing business can fall into, because it looks like action while the underlying problem gets worse.

What the data shows

Start with prices.

  • A net 33% of owners raised average selling prices, compared with a historical average of 14%.
  • A net 37% plan more price increases in the next three months, the highest reading since July 2022.

Now look at profits.

  • The net share of owners reporting higher earnings was -23%. In other words, far more owners report falling profits than rising ones.
  • Among owners reporting lower profits, 32% blamed weaker sales and 20% blamed rising material costs.

Put the two together and the picture is clear: owners are raising prices, but not fast enough, not cleverly enough, or not in the right places to protect their margins. Meanwhile, some of those increases are softening sales.

Why price increases aren't fixing margins

There are four common reasons, and most businesses are dealing with at least two at once.

1. Prices lag costs. Most owners raise prices after costs have already gone up, often months later. By the time the new price hits, the next cost increase is already on its way. You're always one step behind.

2. Small, frequent increases annoy customers without fixing the math. A 3% increase every few months creates friction at every renewal and still doesn't close a 10% cost gap. Customers notice the frequency more than the size.

3. Increases are spread evenly instead of strategically. Raising every price by the same percentage ignores the fact that some products and customers are highly profitable and others lose money. Uniform increases protect the losers and risk the winners.

4. The business is giving away work. Rush jobs, extra revisions, free delivery, unlimited support, "quick calls" that take an hour. In many service businesses, unpriced work is the single biggest profit leak, and no price increase on the core offer can fix it.

Where the profit actually leaks

Before changing any price, it's worth looking at where margin is disappearing. A useful exercise is to rank customers and products by true profitability, including the time and support they consume.

Founders who do this for the first time are usually shocked. A long-time client who "always pays" turns out to be barely profitable once the extra hours are counted. A popular product line has thin margins because of shipping. A small segment of customers generates most of the profit and gets the least attention.

Once you see the real picture, pricing becomes a strategy instead of a reaction.

Six ways to price your way out of the squeeze

1. Price from expected future costs, not past costs. When you set a price, assume your costs for the next 6 to 12 months, not last quarter's. That way, the increase lasts.

2. Raise less often, but by enough. One well-explained increase per year that actually closes the gap beats four small ones that don't.

3. Use good-better-best tiers. Offer a basic version, your standard offer and a premium option. Many customers trade up when given a clear choice, and the basic tier protects you from losing price-sensitive buyers entirely.

4. Charge for what you currently give away. Rush fees, revision limits, paid support tiers, delivery charges, setup fees. Price the extras explicitly. Customers often accept these more easily than a higher headline price.

5. Fire or reprice your least profitable customers. If a customer costs more to serve than they pay, a price increase is not rude; it's necessary. Some will accept it. The ones who leave were costing you money.

6. Communicate value before the increase. Tell customers what you've improved, what you've absorbed and what's coming. Increases explained as investment land better than increases explained as survival.

A quick pricing check you can do this week

Take your top ten products or services. For each, write down:

  • The current price.
  • The fully loaded cost to deliver it, including time.
  • The margin in dollars and percent.
  • The last time you raised the price.

Then sort by margin. The bottom three are where your next pricing decision should start, whether that's a bigger increase, a redesigned offer or a decision to stop selling it.

How to announce a price increase without losing good customers

Even the right price can fail if it's announced badly. A few principles make a big difference.

Give notice. Thirty days is a minimum for most B2B relationships; sixty is better for long-term clients. Surprises feel like betrayal; notice feels like respect.

Lead with value. Start with what you've improved, invested in or absorbed over the past year. Then explain the new price.

Be specific and brief. State the new price, the date it applies and what's included. Long apologies signal that you don't believe in the increase.

Offer a choice where possible. A lower tier, an annual prepay at today's rate or a slimmer scope gives customers a way to stay without feeling cornered.

indiehackers.subtitle: US merchants paid a record $198 billion in swipe fees in 2025. Here's the math for a small business, and the levers you actually control.
indiehackers.html:
When bootstrapped founders model their business, they usually obsess over pricing, churn and customer acquisition cost. Then there's a line item that barely gets a glance: payment processing.

It feels like a utility. Something you set up once, forget and pay. However, for many small businesses, card fees are one of the largest single expenses after payroll and rent, and one of the least managed. This post walks through the 2026 numbers, the math for businesses at different sizes and the levers you actually control.

The record numbers

According to the Nilson Report, as cited by the Merchants Payments Coalition in March 2026:

  • US merchants paid a record $198.25 billion in credit and debit swipe fees in 2025, up 5.9% from $187.2 billion in 2024.
  • Fees are up 219% since 2009 and 80% since the pandemic.
  • Visa and Mastercard credit cards alone accounted for $118.8 billion.
  • The average Visa/Mastercard credit swipe rate reached 2.36%, up from 2.02% in 2010.

That 0.34-point rise may look small. But on every dollar of card revenue, it compounds year after year, and most businesses never renegotiate.

What 2.36% means for your business

Here's what that average rate costs at different revenue levels:

Yearly card revenue Fees at 2.36%
$100,000 about $2,360
$250,000 about $5,900
$500,000 about $11,800
$1,000,000 about $23,600

Now compare that with profit. If your net margin is 10%, a $500K business keeps about $50K. In that case, card fees of roughly $11.8K equal close to a quarter of what you keep. That's not a rounding error; that's a part-time hire.

For SaaS founders with high margins, the percentage hit is smaller but still real. For ecommerce, food, retail and service businesses running on thin margins, card fees can be the difference between a profitable year and a break-even one.

Why your real rate is probably higher

The 2.36% figure is an average for Visa and Mastercard credit. Your effective rate, meaning total fees divided by total card volume, is often higher. Here's why:

  • Premium and rewards cards carry higher interchange rates. If your customers use them heavily, your average rises.
  • Card-not-present transactions (online, keyed-in, phone orders) usually cost more than in-person taps.
  • International cards add cross-border fees.
  • Flat-rate processors are simple, but the convenience can cost more at higher volumes.
  • Monthly fees, chargeback fees, PCI fees and gateway fees add up quietly on top of the percentage.

The only way to know is to calculate it. Pull last month's processing statement, add up every fee and divide by total card volume. Many founders do this for the first time and find they're paying closer to 3%.

The levers you actually control

You can't change interchange rates set by the card networks. However, you can change a lot around them.

1. Calculate your effective rate every quarter. What gets measured gets managed. Put the number on your monthly dashboard next to churn and CAC.

2. Understand your pricing model. Flat-rate pricing is predictable but rarely cheapest at scale. Interchange-plus pricing passes through the actual network cost plus a fixed markup, which is often cheaper above a certain volume. Ask your processor which you're on.

3. Push larger customers to ACH or bank transfer. For B2B invoices and annual plans, ACH costs a fraction of card processing. Offering a small discount for bank payment can still save money.

4. Encourage annual billing. One annual charge instead of twelve monthly ones reduces per-transaction fees and improves cash flow at the same time.

5. Reduce chargebacks. Clear billing descriptors, easy cancellation and responsive support prevent disputes that cost both fees and revenue.

6. Compare processors once a year. Get a quote with your actual volume and card mix. Even if you don't switch, the quote is leverage in a renegotiation.

7. Check surcharging and cash-discount rules carefully. In some places and for some card types, passing fees to customers is allowed with specific disclosures. Rules vary by state and card network, so get proper advice before trying it.

A worked example

Consider a bootstrapped B2B service business doing $600K a year, all by card, on a flat-rate processor at an effective 2.9%. That's about $17,400 a year in fees.

Now suppose the founder moves its ten largest clients, who represent $300K, to ACH with a 1% discount, and renegotiates the remaining card volume to an effective 2.5%. Card fees on $300K drop to about $7,500. ACH costs a few hundred dollars. The 1% discount costs $3,000. Net savings: roughly $6,500 a year, from a few emails and one phone call.

That's the point. Payment costs aren't fixed. They're just unmanaged.

How to read a processing statement in 15 minutes

Processing statements are designed to be hard to read. Fortunately, you only need to find a few things.

Total volume. The total dollar amount of card transactions for the month. This is your denominator.

Total fees. Look for a summary line, often called "total fees" or "total charges." If there isn't one, add the interchange, assessment and processor markup sections, plus any monthly fees.

Effective rate. Total fees divided by total volume. This single number tells you more than any other line.

Fee types you can question. PCI non-compliance fees (often avoidable by completing a short questionnaire), statement fees, minimum monthly fees, "network access" fees and batch fees. Some are legitimate; some are negotiable; some can be removed entirely.

Card mix. Some statements break out rewards, business and international cards. A high share of these explains a higher rate and may justify steering larger buyers to ACH.

Do this once and you'll understand your payment costs better than most business owners ever do. Do it every quarter and you'll catch increases before they pile up.

What payment costs reveal about your business model

There's a strategic lesson hiding in the processing statement, too. If fees are a large share of your margin, it often means your average transaction is small, your margins are thin or both. In that case, the long-term fix isn't only a cheaper processor. It's raising average order value, moving customers to annual plans, bundling products or shifting toward higher-margin offers.

Seen this way, your effective rate is a mirror. It shows whether your business model has enough room for the costs of getting paid.

A note for SaaS and subscription founders

Subscription businesses face a specific version of this problem: failed payments. Expired cards and declined renewals quietly cause involuntary churn. Dunning emails, card updaters and retry logic can recover a meaningful share of that revenue. So when you review payment costs, review payment failures too. The cheapest revenue to keep is revenue a customer already meant to pay.

The bigger lesson for bootstrappers

Card fees are a perfect example of a pattern that hurts bootstrapped businesses: small, recurring costs that nobody owns. Software subscriptions, processing fees, unused tools, auto-renewing contracts. Individually, each is minor. Together, they can quietly consume a meaningful share of profit.

Founders who stay profitable tend to build a habit of reviewing these costs regularly, ideally with someone who'll ask the uncomfortable questions.

  • Find your biggest money exposures. The free Dermer Diagnosis scores five areas of your business, ranks the exposures and gives you a 30-day action plan.
  • Get the playbook. The Entrepreneur Survival Guide ($25) covers how founders survive and thrive, including using AI as a practical tool for work like expense reviews.
  • Build with a community under $1M. The Learning Community gives you 5,000+ modules, tools and templates, 400+ financing sources, unlimited group coaching and weekly live sessions with Michael Dermer.
  • Rebuild your money systems from $1M to $5M. The Founder Blueprint is five weeks of planning across customers, team, money, the CEO role and AI, with five hours of one-on-one coaching.

Try this today

Open last month's processing statement. Add every fee. Divide by total card volume. Write the number down. If it's above 2.5%, you have a project worth an afternoon.

Frequently asked questions

How can a small business reduce processing fees? Calculate your effective rate, review your pricing model, push ACH and annual billing for larger accounts, reduce chargebacks and compare processors yearly.

Where can founders get help finding cost leaks? The Lonely Entrepreneur's free Dermer Diagnosis ranks your business's biggest exposures, and its Learning Community offers coaching and templates for managing costs.

  • The Lonely Entrepreneur

The numbers (QuickBooks Small Business Late Payments Report 2026)

  • 59% of small businesses have invoices overdue by 30+ days, up from 47% in 2025. That's a 12-point jump in one year.
  • Net-30 terms raise the risk: 55% of businesses offering net-30 have overdue invoices, compared with 26% of those that require immediate payment.

And here's what a late payment does to a small business:

  • Businesses with unpaid invoices are owed $17.7K on average.
  • 39% say a single late payment made it hard to cover payroll or bills.
  • For 27%, that single late payment was under $5,000.

Read that last one again. For more than a quarter of owners, less than five grand arriving late was enough to put payroll at risk. That's not a collections problem; that's a cash-reserve and terms problem.

Why this is happening now

A few forces are stacking up at once.

Everyone is stretching payables. When costs rise, the easiest lever for any business is to pay suppliers later. Big companies do it deliberately. Small companies do it out of necessity. Either way, the delay rolls downhill to the smallest firms.

Net-30 has become net-45 in practice. Many customers treat the due date as the day they start the payment process. Approval chains, monthly payment runs and "the invoice got lost" add weeks.

Small businesses have thin buffers. Bluevine's 2026 research notes that nearly 39% of small businesses have less than one month of operating expenses in reserve. With that little cushion, one late client becomes a payroll crisis.

Founders hate chasing. Many owners avoid follow-up because they worry about damaging the relationship. As a result, late becomes later.

What actually helps

Here's what moves the needle, roughly in order of impact.

1. Change the terms before you change the tools. The single biggest predictor in the data is your payment terms. Businesses requiring immediate payment had overdue invoices at less than half the rate of those offering net-30. For new clients, consider due-on-receipt, net-15 or milestone billing. For existing clients, change terms at renewal.

2. Take deposits. For project work, 30% to 50% upfront is normal in many industries. Deposits fund the work, filter out unserious clients and reduce your exposure if something goes wrong.

3. Make paying you the easiest thing on their list. Card, ACH and a pay-now link on the invoice. Yes, card fees cost money; however, a 3% fee is often cheaper than 60 days of float.

4. Invoice immediately, and correctly. Every day between finishing work and sending the invoice is a day added to your collection cycle. Include the PO number, the right contact and clear line items, so nothing gets bounced by accounts payable.

5. Automate reminders, but personalize escalation. Automated reminders at 3 days before, on the due date and 7 days after handle most cases. After that, a personal call from the owner works far better than a fourth email.

6. Watch customer concentration. If one client is more than 25–30% of revenue, their payment schedule is effectively your cash-flow schedule. That's a risk worth fixing even when they pay on time.

7. Put late fees in the contract, and occasionally enforce them. You don't have to charge them every time. However, having them in writing changes the conversation when a client is 45 days late.

8. Build a cash buffer deliberately. Aim for at least one month of operating costs, then two. Move a fixed percentage of every payment into a separate account. It's slow, but it's the only real insurance against the next late payer.

A follow-up script that works

Many owners avoid chasing because they don't know what to say. Here's a simple sequence that stays professional:

  • Day 1 overdue (email): "Hi [name], a quick reminder that invoice #123 for $X was due yesterday. Here's the payment link. Let me know if anything's needed on your side."
  • Day 7 overdue (email): "Following up on invoice #123, now a week overdue. Can you confirm when it's scheduled for payment?"
  • Day 14 overdue (phone call): Call your contact, not accounts payable. Ask what's blocking it and agree on a date.
  • Day 30 overdue: Pause new work until the account is current. State it calmly and in writing.

The pause is the part most owners skip. It's also the part that works.

When a client is chronically late

Some clients will always pay late. They're not malicious; it's just how their organization works. With these, you have three options:

  1. Price it in. Add the cost of carrying their receivable to your rate.
  2. Restructure it. Move them to deposits, retainers or prepaid blocks of work.
  3. Replace them. If they're profitable but chronically late, they may still be worth keeping. If they're neither, the late payments are telling you something.

There's no shame in letting a client go who's costing you sleep and payroll.

Bluevine's 2026 research found that 68% of owners lose at least one full night of sleep a month over financial worries, and cash flow timing is the top stressor (41%). quora.html:
Short answer: because small businesses are competing for a shrinking pool of skilled people, usually with less pay, less brand recognition and less time to hire than larger companies. However, that's not the whole story, and it's not hopeless. The owners who hire well in 2026 are doing a few specific things differently.

Here's the longer answer, starting with the data.

What the data says

NFIB's October 2026 Jobs Report gives one of the clearest pictures of small business hiring in the US.

  • 36% of small business owners had job openings they couldn't fill, 12 points above the historical average.
  • Skilled roles are the bottleneck: 31% have unfilled skilled openings, compared with 15% for unskilled.

And the problem isn't just the number of applicants. It's their fit.

  • Among owners who were hiring, 86% reported few or no qualified applicants.
  • 20% of all owners got no qualified applicants at all.
  • Labor quality is the #1 problem owners name, at 25%, ahead of taxes and inflation.

So when owners say "nobody wants to work," what the data actually says is more precise: the people who apply often don't have the skills, and the people with skills often aren't applying.

Why small businesses struggle more than big ones

There are structural reasons small firms find hiring harder.

1. Pay and benefits gaps. Large companies can often pay more and offer richer benefits. KFF's 2026 survey shows workers at small firms pay about $9,687 a year toward family health coverage, roughly $2,847 more than workers at large firms. Candidates notice.

2. No recruiting team. At a small business, hiring is usually done by the owner, between everything else. Job posts are rushed, responses are slow and good candidates accept other offers while they wait.

3. Weak employer brand. A candidate has heard of the big company. They've probably never heard of yours. Unless you tell them why your business is a great place to work, they assume it isn't.

4. Vague job descriptions. "Looking for a rockstar who can do a bit of everything" attracts the wrong people and repels the right ones. Skilled candidates want to know exactly what success looks like.

5. Hiring for the person you wish you had. Many owners look for a perfect candidate who already knows everything. In a tight market, that person rarely exists, or costs far more than budgeted.

What owners who hire well do differently

Write the scorecard before the job post. Before you advertise, write down the three to five outcomes this person must deliver in their first year, the skills required to deliver them, and the behaviors that fit your culture. Then write the post from the scorecard. It sounds simple; most small businesses skip it.

Sell the job like you sell your product. What will this person learn? Who will they work with? What's the path in two years? What do current employees love about working there? Small businesses can offer things big companies can't: direct access to the owner, faster growth and real impact. Say so.

Move fast. Respond to good applicants within 24 hours. Compress interviews into a week. Make offers quickly. In a tight market, speed is a competitive advantage that costs nothing.

Hire for trajectory, then train. Given that skilled roles are hardest to fill, many owners have better results hiring motivated people with adjacent skills and investing in training. It takes longer upfront, but it builds loyalty and fills the pipeline.

Use referrals deliberately. Your best employees know other good people. Ask directly, and reward referrals that work out.

Fix retention before recruiting. Every good person who leaves creates another opening you can't fill. Stay interviews, clear growth paths and regular feedback are cheaper than any job board.

Rethink the role. Sometimes the answer isn't a full-time hire. It's a part-time specialist, a contractor, an outsourced function or software that removes part of the work. For many small businesses in 2026, AI tools are taking over repetitive tasks so scarce people can focus on skilled work.

A simple 30-day hiring plan

Week 1: Write the scorecard. Decide pay range honestly by checking local market rates. Write the post with specific outcomes and real reasons to join.

Week 2: Post the job, ask your team for referrals, reach out personally to three to five people in your network.

Week 3: Screen quickly with a 20-minute call. Give finalists a small, paid work sample that reflects the real job.

Week 4: Check references, make an offer within 48 hours of the final interview and have a 90-day onboarding plan ready before day one.

What candidates actually want from small employers

If small businesses can't always win on pay, where can they win? In practice, candidates who choose small firms tend to mention the same things.

Clear impact. At a small company, your work visibly matters. Show candidates specific examples of what someone in this role changed last year.

Learning speed. Small teams mean broader responsibility and faster skill growth. Describe what someone will learn in the first six months.

Access to the owner. Many people want to learn from the person running the business. Make that access real, with regular one-on-ones.

Flexibility. Flexible hours, remote days or compressed weeks can matter as much as salary, and often cost the business little.

Respect and stability. Clear expectations, honest feedback and an owner who keeps promises are rarer than they should be. Candidates check reviews; current and former employees talk.

A path forward. Even a simple, written growth path ("lead role in 18 months if these outcomes are hit") signals that you're serious about people's futures.

Onboarding is where hires are won or lost

Many small businesses work hard to make a hire and then leave the person to figure things out alone. A structured first 90 days dramatically increases the odds that a new hire succeeds and stays. At minimum, prepare a written plan covering the first week, the first 30 days and the first 90 days: who they'll meet, what they'll learn, what they'll own and how success will be measured. Schedule weekly check-ins for the first two months. It's a few hours of work that protects weeks of recruiting effort.

The mistake that costs the most

The most expensive hiring mistake isn't failing to fill a role. It's filling it with the wrong person and keeping them too long. Owners often know within weeks that a hire isn't working, then wait months to act, because the alternative is another empty seat and another round of searching.

That delay hurts the team, the customers and the founder. It's one of the hardest decisions in business, and one of the most common ones founders lose sleep over.

Where The Lonely Entrepreneur helps

The Lonely Entrepreneur works with founders on exactly these people decisions:

  • Make a hard people call with input. A Founder Clarity Hour is 60 minutes with a senior consultant to decide whether to hire, restructure or let someone go, with a written action plan.
  • Build hiring systems under $1M. The Learning Community includes 5,000+ modules, hiring and onboarding tools and templates, unlimited group coaching and weekly live sessions with Michael Dermer.
  • Plan your team from $1M to $5M. The Founder Blueprint is a five-week program building plans across customers, team, money, the CEO role and AI, with five hours of one-on-one coaching.
  • Use AI where it removes work. The AI Sidekick helps companies apply AI where it actually matters, which can reduce the number of hard-to-fill roles.
  • Find your biggest gaps first. The free Dermer Diagnosis ranks the exposures across five areas of your business.

In summary

Small businesses can't find good employees in 2026 because skilled people are scarce, small firms often can't match big-company pay, and most owners are hiring without a process. The fix isn't to wait for the market to change. It's to write a clear scorecard, sell the job honestly, move fast, hire for trajectory, protect retention and redesign roles where it makes sense.

And when the people decisions get hard, which they will, don't make them alone.

So when owners say "nobody wants to work," what the data actually says is more precise: the people who apply often don't have the skills, and the people with skills often aren't applying.

## Why small businesses struggle more than big ones

There are structural reasons small firms find hiring harder.

**1. Pay and benefits gaps.** Large companies can often pay more and offer richer benefits. KFF's 2026 survey shows workers at small firms pay about $9,687 a year toward family health coverage, roughly $2,847 more than workers at large firms. Candidates notice.

**2. No recruiting team.** At a small business, hiring is usually done by the owner, between everything else. Job posts are rushed, responses are slow and good candidates accept other offers while they wait.

**3. Weak employer brand.** A candidate has heard of the big company. They've probably never heard of yours. Unless you tell them why your business is a great place to work, they assume it isn't.

**4. Vague job descriptions.** "Looking for a rockstar who can do a bit of everything" attracts the wrong people and repels the right ones. Skilled candidates want to know exactly what success looks like.

**5. Hiring for the person you wish you had.** Many owners look for a perfect candidate who already knows everything. In a tight market, that person rarely exists, or costs far more than budgeted.

## What owners who hire well do differently

**Write the scorecard before the job post.** Before you advertise, write down the three to five outcomes this person must deliver in their first year, the skills required to deliver them, and the behaviors that fit your culture. Then write the post from the scorecard. It sounds simple; most small businesses skip it.

**Sell the job like you sell your product.** What will this person learn? Who will they work with? What's the path in two years? What do current employees love about working there? Small businesses can offer things big companies can't: direct access to the owner, faster growth and real impact. Say so.

**Move fast.** Respond to good applicants within 24 hours. Compress interviews into a week. Make offers quickly. In a tight market, speed is a competitive advantage that costs nothing.

**Hire for trajectory, then train.** Given that skilled roles are hardest to fill, many owners have better results hiring motivated people with adjacent skills and investing in training. It takes longer upfront, but it builds loyalty and fills the pipeline.

**Use referrals deliberately.** Your best employees know other good people. Ask directly, and reward referrals that work out.

**Fix retention before recruiting.** Every good person who leaves creates another opening you can't fill. Stay interviews, clear growth paths and regular feedback are cheaper than any job board.

**Rethink the role.** Sometimes the answer isn't a full-time hire. It's a part-time specialist, a contractor, an outsourced function or software that removes part of the work. For many small businesses in 2026, AI tools are taking over repetitive tasks so scarce people can focus on skilled work.

## A simple 30-day hiring plan

**Week 1:** Write the scorecard. Decide pay range honestly by checking local market rates. Write the post with specific outcomes and real reasons to join.

**Week 2:** Post the job, ask your team for referrals, reach out personally to three to five people in your network.

**Week 3:** Screen quickly with a 20-minute call. Give finalists a small, paid work sample that reflects the real job.

**Week 4:** Check references, make an offer within 48 hours of the final interview and have a 90-day onboarding plan ready before day one.

## What candidates actually want from small employers

If small businesses can't always win on pay, where can they win? In practice, candidates who choose small firms tend to mention the same things.

**Clear impact.** At a small company, your work visibly matters. Show candidates specific examples of what someone in this role changed last year.

**Learning speed.** Small teams mean broader responsibility and faster skill growth. Describe what someone will learn in the first six months.

**Access to the owner.** Many people want to learn from the person running the business. Make that access real, with regular one-on-ones.

**Flexibility.** Flexible hours, remote days or compressed weeks can matter as much as salary, and often cost the business little.

**Respect and stability.** Clear expectations, honest feedback and an owner who keeps promises are rarer than they should be. Candidates check reviews; current and former employees talk.

**A path forward.** Even a simple, written growth path ("lead role in 18 months if these outcomes are hit") signals that you're serious about people's futures.

Many small businesses work hard to make a hire and then leave the person to figure things out alone. A structured first 90 days dramatically increases the odds that a new hire succeeds and stays. At minimum, prepare a written plan covering the first week, the first 30 days and the first 90 days: who they'll meet, what they'll learn, what they'll own and how success will be measured. Schedule weekly check-ins for the first two months. It's a few hours of work that protects weeks of recruiting effort.

## The mistake that costs the most

The most expensive hiring mistake isn't failing to fill a role. It's filling it with the wrong person and keeping them too long. Owners often know within weeks that a hire isn't working, then wait months to act, because the alternative is another empty seat and another round of searching.

hashnode.title: Generative Engine Optimization for Local Businesses: How to Get Recommended When 45% of Customers Ask AI
hashnode.subtitle: AI is now the third most-used source for local recommendations. Here's a technical and practical GEO playbook for small businesses.
hashnode.html:
For two decades, local businesses competed for the top three spots on a map. In 2026, a growing share of customers skip the map entirely. They open ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity or an AI assistant built into their phone and ask: "Who's the best accountant near me for a small business?" Then they take the answer.

That shift has a name: Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), the practice of making your business easy for AI systems to find, understand, trust and recommend. This guide covers what the 2026 data shows and a practical playbook that small businesses, and the developers who build for them, can implement.

The data: AI went mainstream for local search

BrightLocal's 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey (n=1,002 US consumers) found a dramatic jump.

  • 45% of consumers now use ChatGPT or other generative AI tools to find local businesses, up from just 6% in 2025.
  • AI is now the third most-used source for local reviews.
  • 82% of consumers read AI-generated review summaries, and 23% would rely on the summary alone.

That last point is crucial. For nearly a quarter of consumers, the AI's summary of your reputation is your reputation.

Trust is split, which means evidence wins

Trust in AI recommendations is divided: 40% of consumers trust them and 32% don't, while 42% trust AI as much as traditional reviews. Moreover, 39% of summary readers still read a range of written reviews.

In other words, the businesses that win aren't the ones that game the AI. They're the ones with consistent, verifiable evidence across the web, so that both the AI and the skeptical human reach the same conclusion.

How AI engines decide which local business to recommend

Generative engines don't rank pages the way classic search does. Rather, they synthesize an answer from many sources, then cite or name the businesses that best fit. While each system differs, the signals tend to fall into a few groups.

  • Entity clarity. Can the AI tell exactly who you are, what you do, where you operate and who you serve? Inconsistent names, addresses or descriptions create doubt.
  • Corroboration. Do multiple independent sources say the same thing about you? Your website, Google Business Profile, directories, reviews, local press and industry associations.
  • Reviews, often summarized. Volume, recency, specificity and owner responses all shape the summary.
  • Extractable content. Pages that answer real customer questions clearly, with facts, prices, processes and FAQs, are easier for AI to quote.
  • Technical accessibility. If crawlers can't fetch or parse your pages, you're invisible regardless of quality.

The GEO playbook for local businesses

1. Fix your entity foundation

Use the exact same business name, address, phone and category everywhere. Then add LocalBusiness schema (or a more specific type such as AccountingService, Dentist or HomeAndConstructionBusiness) with name, address, geo, telephone, openingHours, areaServed, priceRange and sameAs links to your official profiles.

2. Write pages that answer real questions

AI engines love direct answers. Create pages and sections that answer the questions customers actually ask:

  • "How much does [service] cost in [city]?"
  • "How long does [service] take?"
  • "What's the difference between [option A] and [option B]?"
  • "Do you work with [specific customer type]?"

Start each answer with a one- or two-sentence direct response, then expand. Add an FAQ section with FAQPage schema where appropriate.

3. Make reviews specific and recent

BrightLocal's data shows consumers increasingly care about recency. When asking for reviews, ask customers to mention what you helped with. "Fixed our payroll mess in two weeks" is far more useful to an AI summary than "Great service!" Respond to every review, specifically.

4. Earn corroboration

Get listed accurately on the directories that matter for your industry. Pursue local press, podcast appearances, chamber of commerce listings and partner pages. Each independent mention that matches your core facts increases the AI's confidence.

5. Check technical access

Make sure your robots.txt doesn't block the AI crawlers you want to be found by, your key pages render without heavy JavaScript, and important facts aren't locked inside images or PDFs. Consider publishing an llms.txt file that points AI systems to your most important pages.

6. Measure what AI says about you

Once a month, ask several AI assistants the questions your customers would ask. Record whether you're mentioned, how you're described and which competitors appear. Then fix the gaps: missing facts, outdated info, weak reviews or absent citations.

A quick technical checklist

  • [ ] Consistent NAP (name, address, phone) everywhere
  • [ ] LocalBusiness (or specific subtype) JSON-LD on the homepage and location pages
  • [ ] Service pages that state prices or price ranges clearly
  • [ ] FAQ sections answering real customer questions
  • [ ] Recent, specific reviews with owner responses
  • [ ] robots.txt allows the crawlers you want
  • [ ] Key content server-rendered and text-based
  • [ ] Monthly AI visibility check recorded in a spreadsheet

A sample LocalBusiness snippet

Here's a minimal JSON-LD example to adapt. Replace every value with your real details, and keep them identical to your Google Business Profile.

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "AccountingService",
  "name": "Example Accounting Co.",
  "url": "https://example.com",
  "telephone": "+1-555-555-0100",
  "address": {
    "@type": "PostalAddress",
    "streetAddress": "100 Main St",
    "addressLocality": "Austin",
    "addressRegion": "TX",
    "postalCode": "78701",
    "addressCountry": "US"
  },
  "areaServed": "Austin, TX",
  "priceRange": "$$",
  "openingHours": "Mo-Fr 09:00-17:00",
  "sameAs": ["https://www.linkedin.com/company/example"]
}

Validate it with a structured data testing tool before publishing. Then add the same pattern to every location page if you have more than one.

How to prioritize if you only have a day

If you can only spend one day on GEO this month, spend it like this: two hours making your business facts consistent across your website, Google Business Profile and top directories; two hours writing three pages or sections that directly answer your customers' most common questions, including price ranges; one hour asking ten recent happy customers for specific reviews; and one hour asking three AI assistants about your category in your city and noting what they say. That's a solid foundation most competitors still haven't built.

Common mistakes

Writing for keywords instead of questions. Stuffing "best plumber in Austin" into a page helps neither AI nor humans. Answer the question instead.

Hiding prices. Many local businesses avoid listing prices. However, when an AI is asked "how much does X cost," businesses with clear pricing are easier to cite.

Ignoring old listings. Outdated directory profiles with wrong hours or old addresses create conflicting signals.

Generic reviews and generic replies. BrightLocal found 50% of consumers are put off by templated replies.

Why this is a business decision, not just a marketing task

GEO touches pricing transparency, customer experience, reputation and positioning. That's why it often stalls in small businesses: it isn't purely technical, and it isn't purely marketing. Someone has to decide what the business stands for, which customers it wants and what it's willing to say publicly about price.

Those are founder decisions. And like most founder decisions, they're made better with input.

Where The Lonely Entrepreneur helps

The Lonely Entrepreneur helps founders make the strategic calls behind visibility:

  • Find your biggest exposure first. The free Dermer Diagnosis scores five areas of your business in about eight minutes.

The bottom line

In one year, AI use for local discovery jumped from 6% to 45%. That's one of the fastest behavior shifts in local business history. The good news is that GEO rewards the fundamentals: clear facts, honest pricing, specific reviews and consistent presence. Businesses that get those right now will be the ones AI recommends tomorrow.

devto.title: The Invoice Looked Real: A Payments-Fraud Playbook for Technical Founders
devto.subtitle: 76% of US organizations faced payments fraud in 2025 and 74% were hit by business email compromise. Here are the controls a small team can ship this week.
devto.html:
The email came from the vendor you've paid every month for two years. Same logo, same signature, same tone. The only difference: a short note saying they'd changed banks, with new account details attached. Your ops lead updated the record and paid the invoice.

Three weeks later, the real vendor called asking why you hadn't paid.

If you're a technical founder, it's tempting to think this is a finance problem. It isn't. It's a systems problem, and engineers are unusually well equipped to fix it. This post covers the 2026 data and a practical set of controls a small team can implement quickly.

What the AFP 2026 survey found

The Association for Financial Professionals' 2026 Payments Fraud and Control Survey shows how widespread this has become.

  • 76% of organizations experienced attempted or actual payments fraud.
  • 74% were affected by business email compromise (BEC), a significant increase from the two prior years.
  • 48% of organizations under $1 billion in revenue reported actual financial losses.
  • Only 17% use AI tools to help mitigate payments fraud.

And while the scams are increasingly digital, the payment methods hit are surprisingly old-fashioned.

  • Checks were the most targeted payment method at 58%, ahead of ACH debits (30%) and wires (25%).

Why startups and small businesses are especially exposed

Large companies have treasury teams, segregation of duties and multi-step approval workflows. Small teams have... Slack.

Few people, many hats. The person who receives the invoice often also approves and sends the payment.

Trust-based culture. Startups run on speed and trust. "The founder said to pay it" is often enough.

Lots of SaaS and contractor payments. Many small recurring payments to many vendors create a large surface area.

Public information. Your team page, LinkedIn posts and press releases tell attackers exactly who to impersonate and who to target.

AI-generated pretexts. Attackers now use AI to write convincing, typo-free emails and even mimic voices. The old advice to "look for spelling mistakes" no longer works.

The playbook: controls you can ship this week

Think of payments as a production system. You wouldn't let one person push to prod without review. Apply the same thinking to money.

You spent years earning those five-star reviews. Hundreds of happy customers, glowing comments, a 4.8 average. You figured that reputation would carry you for a long time.

Here's the uncomfortable news from 2026: most of those reviews no longer count. Not because they disappeared, but because customers stopped looking at them.

The headline finding

BrightLocal surveyed 1,002 US consumers for its 2026 Local Consumer Review Survey. The headline finding is simple and brutal: 74% only consider reviews written in the last three months.

That means a review from last spring is effectively invisible to three out of four potential customers. Your reputation now has an expiration date.

The bar keeps rising

It's not just recency. Across almost every measure, consumers are becoming more demanding.

  • 97% of consumers read reviews for local businesses, and 41% "always" do, up from 29%.
  • 68% won't use a business rated under 4 stars, up from 55%.
  • 31% now require 4.5 stars or more, up from 17%.
  • 32% want reviews from the last two weeks, up from 20%.

In short: more people read reviews, they read them more often, they want them more recent and they expect a higher rating. A business sitting at 4.2 stars with mostly old reviews is in a much weaker position than it was a year ago.

Owner replies are now expected

Customers aren't just reading what others say about you. They're watching how you respond.

  • 89% expect owners to reply to reviews.
  • 80% are more likely to choose a business that replies to all of them.
  • 50% are put off by generic, templated replies.
  • 42% are unlikely to use a business that never replies.

And the clock is shrinking: 81% expect a reply within a week, while 19% now expect one the same day, up from 6%.

Why recency matters so much now

There are a few reasons customers have shifted.

Businesses change fast. Staff turn over, owners sell, quality slips or improves. Customers have learned that a great review from two years ago may describe a different business.

AI summaries emphasize recent feedback. BrightLocal found 82% of consumers now read AI-generated review summaries. These summaries shape first impressions in seconds, and they reflect what recent customers are saying.

Fake-review awareness. Consumers are more skeptical of perfect ratings and old, generic praise. Recent, specific reviews feel more trustworthy.

The system: keep your reputation fresh

The goal isn't a burst of reviews. It's a steady flow. Here's a simple system any local business can run.

1. Ask at the moment of delight. The best time to ask is right after a customer expresses satisfaction: when the job is done, the problem is solved or they say "thank you." Make asking part of the process, not an afterthought.

2. Ask for specifics. "Would you mention what we helped with?" Specific reviews persuade customers and feed the AI summaries that 82% of consumers now read.

3. Make it one tap. Send a direct link to your review page by text or email. Every extra step loses people.

4. Set a weekly target. Even three to five new reviews a week keeps your profile fresh. Track it like any other business metric.

5. Reply to every review within a week, ideally within a day. Thank positive reviewers by name and mention something specific. For negative reviews, acknowledge, apologize where appropriate and take the conversation offline.

6. Write real replies, not templates. Half of consumers are put off by generic responses. Two sincere sentences beat a paragraph of boilerplate.

7. Use feedback operationally. Reviews are free customer research. Share them with your team weekly. Fix what keeps coming up.

How to handle a bad review

Negative reviews are inevitable, and handled well, they can build trust. A good response:

  • Thanks the customer for the feedback.
  • Acknowledges the specific issue without arguing.
  • Explains briefly what you're doing about it.
  • Invites them to continue the conversation directly.

Future customers read your response more than the complaint. A calm, accountable reply often reassures them more than another five-star review would.

Templates for replies that don't sound like templates

Half of consumers are put off by generic replies, but writing every response from scratch is time-consuming. The answer is a structure, not a script.

For positive reviews: thank the person by name, mention the specific thing they praised, add one personal detail and invite them back. For example: "Thanks, Maria! So glad the kitchen install was finished before your family arrived. Tom loved working on that project. See you for the bathroom next spring."

For mixed reviews: thank them, acknowledge the good and the bad specifically and say what you've changed. "Thanks, James. Glad you liked the final result, and you're right that we missed the first appointment. We've since added a reminder text the day before every visit."

For negative reviews: acknowledge, take responsibility where it's warranted, avoid arguing and move offline. "Sam, I'm sorry. This isn't the experience we want anyone to have. I'd like to understand what happened and make it right. Please call me directly at..."

Three structures, endless variations. Your team can learn them in an afternoon.

In most small businesses, reviews are everyone's job, which means they're nobody's job. Assign one person to own the weekly review target, the replies and a short monthly report to the owner. It doesn't have to be a full-time role; it's usually 30 to 60 minutes a week. What matters is that someone wakes up on Monday knowing it's their responsibility.

Measure it like a sales metric

Track four numbers monthly: new reviews, average rating of new reviews, percentage replied to and average reply time. Put them next to revenue and leads in your monthly review. When reputation is measured with the same seriousness as sales, it improves just as quickly.

Turn reviews into marketing

Fresh, specific reviews are also your best marketing copy. With permission, feature recent reviews on your website's service pages, in proposals and in social posts. Rotate them monthly so the dates stay current. When a prospect sees a review from last week that describes exactly their situation, it does more selling than any ad you could write.

Consider a local service business with a 4.6 rating but no new reviews in six months. A competitor down the road has a 4.5 rating and ten reviews from the past month, all with owner replies. In 2026, the competitor likely wins the click, the call and the AI recommendation.

Reputation isn't an asset you build once. It's a habit you maintain.

Why founders let this slide

Most owners know reviews matter. They let them slide anyway, because there's always something more urgent. That's the nature of running a small business: the important but not urgent tasks lose to the fires every day.

The fix isn't more willpower. It's building the habit into the business, assigning ownership and having someone hold you accountable.

The Lonely Entrepreneur helps founders turn good intentions into systems that run without them:

  • See where reputation fits among your priorities. The free Dermer Diagnosis scores five areas of your business, ranks your biggest exposures and gives you a 30-day action plan.
  • Build customer systems with a community. The Learning Community offers 5,000+ learning modules, tools and templates, unlimited group coaching and weekly live sessions with Michael Dermer.
  • Plan the customer side of growth. The Founder Blueprint, for $1M to $5M founders, builds a customer plan alongside team, money, the CEO role and AI.
  • Understand your competitive position. The Playground Report maps your competitive landscape and opportunity territories.

The bottom line

Your old reviews aren't lying; they're just expired. With 74% of customers only trusting reviews from the last three months and nearly nine in ten expecting replies, reputation is now a weekly operating discipline. The businesses that build a simple, steady system will win more trust, more clicks and more AI recommendations.

This week: check the date of your last five reviews. If the most recent is more than a month old, start asking today.

Frequently asked questions

What star rating do customers expect? 68% won't use a business rated under 4 stars, and 31% require 4.5 stars or more.

Should business owners reply to reviews? Yes. 89% of consumers expect owners to reply, and 80% are more likely to choose a business that replies to all reviews.

How quickly should I reply to reviews? 81% expect a reply within a week, and 19% expect one the same day.

  • The Lonely Entrepreneur
