wordpress.html:
For many small business owners, tariffs used to be something that happened to other people: big manufacturers, global retailers, companies with import departments. In 2026, that's no longer true. Tariffs now show up in the price of packaging, equipment, parts, ingredients and inventory for businesses that have never imported anything directly.

The latest NFIB data shows just how widely the impact has spread, and how owners are responding. This article walks through the numbers, the trade-offs and a practical plan for protecting your margins.

What NFIB's 2026 Tariff Report found

NFIB surveyed its members specifically about tariffs and trade policy. The results are stark.

  • 56% say tariffs have hurt their business; only 8% report a positive effect.

Among owners who were affected, the effects cascaded through the business.

  • 78% saw higher supply prices.
  • 63% raised their own prices, and 58% accepted lower profits.
  • 18% changed vendors, and 16% cut employees in response.

Meanwhile, research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that about 80% of goods and retail firms passed some costs on to customers, while about 60% absorbed some themselves.

In other words, most businesses are doing both at the same time: raising prices and eating part of the cost. That's the trap. Pass on too much and you lose customers; absorb too much and you lose the business.

The indirect hit most owners miss

Many owners assume they're not exposed because they don't import. However, tariff costs travel through supply chains. Your distributor imports. Your equipment supplier uses imported components. Your packaging vendor buys imported materials. Each one passes on part of their cost to you, often with little explanation.

The Federal Reserve's 2026 Report on Employer Firms reinforces this: 77% of employer firms named rising costs or tariff-related costs as a financial challenge, with retail (69%) and manufacturing (62%) hit hardest by tariff costs specifically.

That's why the first step isn't a strategy. It's visibility.

Step 1: Map your exposure

Before you can respond, you need to know where tariff costs are entering your business. Here's a simple process:

  1. List your top 20 cost items by annual spend.
  2. For each, ask your supplier directly: how much of this is imported or contains imported components? Have tariffs affected your price, and do you expect further increases?
  3. Calculate the increase for each item compared with a year ago.
  4. Rank by impact: annual spend times percentage increase.

Most owners find that a handful of items drive most of the exposure. That's where to focus.

Step 2: Decide who pays, item by item

There's no single right answer about passing costs on. Instead, the decision should vary by product, customer and competitive position.

Pass it on where you have pricing power. Specialized products, strong relationships, little direct competition or customers who value reliability over price.

Absorb it where the customer is price-sensitive and the product drives other sales. A loss leader or entry product might be worth protecting if it brings customers to higher-margin offers.

Redesign it where neither works. Change the specification, package size, bundle or service level so the economics work again.

Drop it where it no longer makes sense. Some products may simply become unprofitable. Removing them can free up cash and attention.

Step 3: Strengthen your supply chain

Diversify carefully. Changing vendors (as 18% of owners did) can help, but test quality and reliability with small orders first. A cheaper supplier who misses deadlines can cost more than the tariff.

Negotiate. Your suppliers are under pressure too, but many have room. Ask for longer price locks, volume discounts, better payment terms or shared absorption of increases.

Consider domestic or nearshore alternatives. They may cost more on paper but reduce tariff risk, shipping delays and inventory requirements.

Revisit inventory strategy. Some businesses buy ahead of expected increases; others reduce inventory to limit exposure. Both can be right, depending on your cash position and how confident you are about future prices.

Step 4: Communicate with customers

Customers are more accepting of increases when they understand them. Be honest without being dramatic. A short note explaining that costs for specific inputs have risen, what you've absorbed and what's changing tends to land better than a silent price hike.

For B2B customers, consider adding price-adjustment clauses to contracts tied to specific input costs. It protects you from being locked into unprofitable pricing if tariffs rise again.

Step 5: Protect the people decision

The data shows 16% of affected owners cut employees. Sometimes that's unavoidable. However, it should be the last lever, not the first. Before cutting people, check whether pricing, product mix, supplier negotiations or reducing other fixed costs can close the gap. Good people are hard to find, and NFIB's own data shows 36% of owners can't fill open jobs. Losing someone now can be very expensive to reverse later.

A scenario worth working through

Consider a small specialty food producer with $2.4M in revenue. Packaging and two key ingredients rose 14% due to tariffs, adding about $110,000 in annual costs. Profit before the increase: $190,000.

Option C, the strategic route: raise prices 7% on the premium line where customers are loyal, keep entry products flat, switch one ingredient to a domestic supplier at a 6% saving, and shrink one package size. The result recovers most of the cost while protecting the products that bring in new customers.

The best answer is rarely one lever. It's a combination, chosen deliberately.

Tariffs don't only squeeze margins; they squeeze cash. Higher input costs mean more money tied up in inventory and receivables before customers pay you back. Update your cash forecast with the new cost levels, check whether your credit line still covers the gap and be cautious about buying large amounts of inventory ahead of expected increases unless the cash position can comfortably handle it. Many businesses that survive a margin hit get into trouble because they ran out of cash first.

Why tariff decisions are so hard

Tariff policy can change quickly. Owners are making long-term decisions about pricing, suppliers and staff based on rules that might shift next quarter. That uncertainty pushes many founders into paralysis or panic.

The way through is the same as with any uncertain decision: make choices that work across several scenarios, keep them reversible where possible, and test your thinking with people who've dealt with similar shocks.

  • Navigate it with peers. The Learning Community includes 5,000+ modules, tools and templates, 400+ financing sources, unlimited group coaching and weekly live sessions with Michael Dermer.

  • Rebuild the plan from $1M to $5M. The Founder Blueprint covers customers, team, money, the CEO role and AI.
  • Get a senior partner from $5M to $50M. Sidekick offers weekly check-ins on CEO-level decisions.

The bottom line

More than half of small businesses say tariffs have hurt them. Most are raising prices and absorbing costs at the same time, often without a clear plan. The owners who come through best will map their exposure, decide who pays item by item, strengthen their supply chain, communicate honestly and protect their people as long as they reasonably can.

This week: list your top 20 cost items and ask each supplier one question: how have tariffs affected your price, and what do you expect next?

How are owners responding to tariffs? Among affected owners, 78% saw higher supply prices, 63% raised prices, 58% accepted lower profits, 18% changed vendors and 16% cut employees.

blogger.subtitle: KFF's 2026 data shows small businesses and their people carry a heavier health-cost burden than big companies. Here's how owners can compete for talent without breaking the budget.
blogger.html:
Ask a small business owner what keeps them up at night, and health insurance is often near the top of the list. It's one of the largest costs after payroll, it rises almost every year and it directly affects whether you can hire and keep good people.

The 2026 data confirms what many owners feel: small businesses, and the people who work for them, are carrying a heavier burden than their counterparts at large companies. This article walks through the numbers, why the gap exists and what owners can realistically do about it.

What KFF's 2026 survey found

KFF's 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey is the most widely cited benchmark for employer health costs in the US. The headline numbers:

  • The average family premium reached $28,303, up 5%.
  • Workers' share of family premiums rose 9% to $7,471 on average.

But the averages hide a big difference between small and large employers.

  • Workers at small firms (under 200 employees) pay $9,687 a year for family coverage, about $2,847 more than workers at large firms.

  • Small-firm single-coverage deductibles average $2,624, compared with $1,772 at large firms.
  • 32% of covered small-firm workers pay more than half of the family premium, compared with 6% at large firms.

Put simply, a worker at a small firm often pays more out of each paycheck and more when they actually use their coverage.

Why small firms pay more

The gap isn't because small business owners care less about their people. It's structural.

Smaller risk pools. Large employers spread costs over thousands of employees. A small group's premiums can swing sharply based on a few people's health needs.

Less negotiating power. Big companies negotiate directly with insurers, often self-insure and have benefits teams to manage costs. Small businesses usually buy off-the-shelf plans.

Administrative costs. The fixed cost of administering a plan is spread over fewer people.

Tighter budgets. Many small businesses can afford to cover a share of the premium but not the full family cost, so more of it lands on employees.

Why it matters beyond the budget

Health benefits are a hiring and retention issue, not just a cost line. NFIB's October 2026 data shows 36% of owners have openings they can't fill, and skilled roles are hardest. When a candidate compares an offer from a small firm with one from a large company, a $2,800 annual difference in health costs is real money.

The burden also hits owners personally. Patriot Software's 2026 survey of 1,000 owners found 24.6% have delayed or gone without health insurance because of business costs, rising to 37.7% among new owners. And 29.4% named affordable healthcare as the single most meaningful fix for burnout.

Options owners should know about

The right approach depends on your size, location, workforce and budget. Here are the main options to discuss with a licensed benefits advisor.

1. Re-shop and re-structure your current plan. Compare carriers and plan designs every year. Adjusting deductibles, networks or contribution levels can sometimes reduce costs without gutting coverage.

2. Health Reimbursement Arrangements (HRAs). Arrangements such as the Individual Coverage HRA (ICHRA) and the Qualified Small Employer HRA (QSEHRA) let employers reimburse employees tax-free for individual health insurance up to a set amount. They offer predictable costs for the employer and choice for employees, though rules and eligibility apply.

3. Level-funded plans. Some small groups can use partially self-funded, level-funded arrangements that may return surplus if claims are low. They carry more complexity and risk, so understand the terms.

4. Professional Employer Organizations (PEOs). By pooling employees from many companies, PEOs can sometimes offer larger-company benefits and rates. Fees and fit vary.

5. Association or group options. Depending on your industry and state, associations or chambers may offer group plans.

6. Supplemental benefits. Dental, vision, telehealth, mental health support and HSA contributions can increase perceived value at relatively low cost.

Always get advice from a licensed broker or benefits professional; rules differ by state and change frequently.

Compete on the whole package

Even if you can't match a big company's health plan, you can compete on the full employment package. Many employees weigh these as heavily as benefits:

  • Flexibility: remote days, flexible hours or compressed weeks.
  • Growth: faster responsibility, clear career paths and training.
  • Culture: access to leadership, real impact and respect.
  • Transparency: clearly explaining what the business contributes toward benefits and why.

A simple total-compensation statement showing salary, the employer's health contribution, retirement contributions and other benefits often surprises employees, who rarely see the full value.

A practical annual benefits review

Once a year, before renewal, run through these questions:

  1. What did we spend in total on health benefits, and how much did that increase?
  2. What do employees pay for single and family coverage, and how does that compare with the KFF small-firm averages?
  3. Have we compared at least three alternatives, including an HRA or PEO option?
  4. What do employees actually value? Have we asked them?
  5. How are benefits affecting hiring and retention?

Treat it as a strategic decision, not an administrative renewal.

The scenario most owners face

Consider a 22-person firm whose renewal comes in 11% higher. The owner can absorb the increase, pass more of it to employees, cut plan quality or explore alternatives. Absorbing it costs margin. Passing it on hurts retention. Cutting quality may lose key people with families.

Exploring alternatives might reveal that an ICHRA gives employees more choice at a similar cost, or that a PEO offers better rates, or that a modest plan change plus an HSA contribution keeps everyone roughly whole. The point is that the default, signing the renewal, is rarely the best option. It's just the easiest.

How to talk to employees about benefits costs

When costs rise, how you communicate matters almost as much as the decision itself. Explain what the business pays and what employees pay, in dollars. Share what you compared and why you chose the option you did. Give people time before open enrollment to ask questions. If contributions are increasing, say so plainly and explain what you did to limit the increase. Employees generally understand that health costs rise; what damages trust is surprise and silence.

Why owners need better input on this

Benefits decisions combine money, people, regulation and ethics. Owners care about their employees and feel responsible for their families' health. At the same time, they have to keep the business viable. It's one of those decisions where the founder often feels completely alone: brokers sell plans, employees want more and the numbers don't seem to work.

  • Get a senior partner from $5M to $50M. Sidekick supports CEO-level decisions with weekly check-ins.

The bottom line

Small-firm workers pay about $9,687 a year for family coverage, nearly $2,850 more than large-firm workers, and face higher deductibles. That gap affects hiring, retention and owners' own wellbeing. Ask a small business owner what keeps them up at night, and health insurance is often near the top of the list. It's one of the largest costs after payroll, it rises almost every year and it directly affects whether you can hire and keep good people.

KFF's 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey is the most widely cited benchmark for employer health costs in the US. The headline numbers:

- The average family premium reached **$28,303**, up 5%.
- Workers' share of family premiums rose **9% to $7,471** on average.

But the averages hide a big difference between small and large employers.

![What workers pay for family coverage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mohamedsaidyekhlef-png/mohamedsaidyekhlef-png/tle-media/charts/c12a.jpg)

- Workers at **small firms (under 200 employees) pay $9,687 a year** for family coverage, about **$2,847 more** than workers at large firms.

![The small-firm penalty](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mohamedsaidyekhlef-png/mohamedsaidyekhlef-png/tle-media/charts/c12b.jpg)

- Small-firm single-coverage deductibles average **$2,624**, compared with $1,772 at large firms.
- **32% of covered small-firm workers** pay more than half of the family premium, compared with **6%** at large firms.

Put simply, a worker at a small firm often pays more out of each paycheck *and* more when they actually use their coverage.

## Why small firms pay more

The gap isn't because small business owners care less about their people. It's structural.

**Smaller risk pools.** Large employers spread costs over thousands of employees. A small group's premiums can swing sharply based on a few people's health needs.

**Less negotiating power.** Big companies negotiate directly with insurers, often self-insure and have benefits teams to manage costs. Small businesses usually buy off-the-shelf plans.

**Administrative costs.** The fixed cost of administering a plan is spread over fewer people.

**Tighter budgets.** Many small businesses can afford to cover a share of the premium but not the full family cost, so more of it lands on employees.

## Why it matters beyond the budget

Health benefits are a hiring and retention issue, not just a cost line. NFIB's October 2026 data shows **36% of owners have openings they can't fill**, and skilled roles are hardest. When a candidate compares an offer from a small firm with one from a large company, a $2,800 annual difference in health costs is real money.

The burden also hits owners personally. Patriot Software's 2026 survey of 1,000 owners found **24.6% have delayed or gone without health insurance because of business costs**, rising to 37.7% among new owners. And **29.4%** named affordable healthcare as the single most meaningful fix for burnout.

## Options owners should know about

The right approach depends on your size, location, workforce and budget. Here are the main options to discuss with a licensed benefits advisor.

**1. Re-shop and re-structure your current plan.** Compare carriers and plan designs every year. Adjusting deductibles, networks or contribution levels can sometimes reduce costs without gutting coverage.

**2. Health Reimbursement Arrangements (HRAs).** Arrangements such as the Individual Coverage HRA (ICHRA) and the Qualified Small Employer HRA (QSEHRA) let employers reimburse employees tax-free for individual health insurance up to a set amount. They offer predictable costs for the employer and choice for employees, though rules and eligibility apply.

**3. Level-funded plans.** Some small groups can use partially self-funded, level-funded arrangements that may return surplus if claims are low. They carry more complexity and risk, so understand the terms.

**4. Professional Employer Organizations (PEOs).** By pooling employees from many companies, PEOs can sometimes offer larger-company benefits and rates. Fees and fit vary.

**5. Association or group options.** Depending on your industry and state, associations or chambers may offer group plans.

**6. Supplemental benefits.** Dental, vision, telehealth, mental health support and HSA contributions can increase perceived value at relatively low cost.

Always get advice from a licensed broker or benefits professional; rules differ by state and change frequently.

## Compete on the whole package

Even if you can't match a big company's health plan, you can compete on the full employment package. Many employees weigh these as heavily as benefits:

- **Flexibility:** remote days, flexible hours or compressed weeks.
- **Growth:** faster responsibility, clear career paths and training.
- **Culture:** access to leadership, real impact and respect.
- **Transparency:** clearly explaining what the business contributes toward benefits and why.

A simple total-compensation statement showing salary, the employer's health contribution, retirement contributions and other benefits often surprises employees, who rarely see the full value.

## A practical annual benefits review

Once a year, before renewal, run through these questions:

1. What did we spend in total on health benefits, and how much did that increase?
2. What do employees pay for single and family coverage, and how does that compare with the KFF small-firm averages?

tumblr.subtitle: 84% of owners have sacrificed their health, relationships or wellbeing for the business. Here's what the data says, and how to build a company that doesn't consume you.
tumblr.html:
There's a story founders tell about themselves. It goes like this: real entrepreneurs sacrifice. They sleep less, work weekends, skip vacations and push through. The exhaustion is proof of commitment. The burnout is a badge.

It's a compelling story. It's also wrong, and the 2026 data shows what it costs.

The numbers behind the badge

Patriot Software surveyed 1,000 current and recent small business owners in 2026. The findings are sobering.

84.4% have sacrificed their health, relationships or mental wellbeing for their business. Only 15.4% report no significant sacrifices.

What did they give up? 45.8% sacrificed family time, 42.2% physical health, 41.4% hobbies, 40.9% mental health and 35.1% friendships.

And the day-to-day reality looks like this:

  • 53.5% lose sleep over their business at least a few times a week.
  • 47.7% have skipped or delayed their own paycheck.
  • Only 22.5% describe their mental health as thriving.

Bluevine's separate 2026 research adds that 68% of owners lose at least one full night of sleep a month over financial worries, and 53% say financial stress left them emotionally drained or burned out in the past year.

These aren't the numbers of people wearing a badge. They're the numbers of people quietly running out of fuel.

The hardest-hit founders

Burnout isn't evenly spread. In the Patriot survey, 29.6% of new owners (under a year) lose sleep almost every night, compared with 12.7% of veteran owners. Gen Z owners report the most strain: 65.7% describe themselves as in survival mode, and 49.3% say they've sacrificed their mental health.

Yet there's something remarkable in the data, too. 73% still believe in entrepreneurship. 30.8% love it and can't imagine doing anything else, and 42.2% believe in it but are exhausted.

That's the heart of it. Most founders don't want to quit. They want to keep going without losing themselves.

Why founders burn out

Burnout isn't simply working too many hours. It's a mix of factors that compound.

Unrelenting responsibility. Everything ends with you: payroll, customers, problems, decisions. There's no "off" switch when the business is your name and your savings.

Financial pressure. Cash flow worries were the top stressor in Bluevine's research (41%), followed by paying monthly bills (39%). When personal finances are tied to the business, every bad month feels existential.

Isolation. Founders often hide the strain from their team, their family and their peers. The weight gets heavier precisely because nobody else is carrying any of it.

No recovery. Rest gets postponed until "things calm down," which they rarely do. Without recovery, stress accumulates.

Identity fusion. When the business is who you are, every setback feels personal, and stepping away feels like failure.

Signs you're closer to empty than you think

Burnout often creeps in slowly. Watch for:

  • Feeling detached or cynical about work you used to care about.
  • Constant fatigue that sleep doesn't fix.
  • Irritability with your team, customers or family.
  • Avoiding decisions or emails you'd normally handle easily.
  • Losing interest in things outside work.
  • Physical symptoms: headaches, poor sleep, getting sick more often.

If several of these sound familiar, it's not a weakness. It's information.

What actually helps

There's no single cure, but founders who recover and sustain themselves tend to do a few things.

1. Treat your energy as a business asset. You'd never run a machine without maintenance. Schedule rest, exercise and time off as non-negotiable, like payroll.

2. Pay yourself, even a little. Patriot found 47.7% of owners skip or delay pay. A consistent owner's salary, even a modest one, reduces personal financial stress and shows you the true economics of the business.

3. Remove one thing every week. Delegate, automate or stop at least one recurring task. Small reductions compound.

4. Fix the cash-flow worry at its source. Deposits, shorter terms, a 13-week forecast and a small reserve address the top stressor directly.

5. Build boundaries your team can see. Set hours when you're not available. When the founder models sustainable work, the team follows.

6. Talk to people who get it. Founder peers who've been through it can normalize what you're feeling and share what helped. This is often the most powerful step, and the one most founders delay.

7. Get professional support. If you're experiencing persistent anxiety, depression or exhaustion, talk to a doctor or mental health professional. It's one of the best investments you'll make in your business.

What changes when founders stop hiding it

One of the most striking patterns in founder communities is what happens when someone finally says out loud, "I'm not okay." Almost always, someone else in the room says, "Me neither," and then shares what helped them. YouGov's research for the Start Up Loans Company found that 59% of owners feel more connected when they know other leaders share their experiences.

That connection doesn't fix cash flow or remove hard decisions. But it changes how heavy they feel. It turns a private crisis into a shared problem with practical answers. And it gives founders permission to rest, delegate and ask for help without feeling like they're failing.

A note for founders' families

If you love someone running a business, you've probably seen the late nights, the distracted dinners and the stress they try to hide. A few things help: ask about the business without trying to fix it, encourage them to find founder peers who can share the load, protect some time that's completely off-limits for work and notice when exhaustion turns into something more serious. Your support matters more than you may realize, even when they don't say so.

The difference between a hard season and a broken system

Every business has hard seasons: a launch, a bad quarter, a key person leaving. Pushing hard for a few weeks can be necessary. The problem is when the "season" never ends. If you've been in survival mode for a year, it's not a season anymore. It's how the business is designed, and design can be changed.

Building a business that doesn't consume you

Ultimately, preventing burnout isn't only about self-care. It's about business design. A company that depends on the founder for everything will exhaust the founder, no matter how many yoga classes they take.

That means building systems, hiring and developing people, creating predictable cash flow and making decisions with input instead of alone. These are business problems with business solutions, and they're exactly the problems The Lonely Entrepreneur was built to address.

A small exercise for this week

Write down three things: the one task that drains you most, the one decision you've been avoiding and the one person who has been through something similar. Then do something about one of them before Friday. Not all three. One.

Where The Lonely Entrepreneur helps

Michael Dermer founded The Lonely Entrepreneur after building a company to 1,000 employees and experiencing the founder's isolation firsthand. TLE has since helped more than 500,000 founders. Here's how it helps founders running on empty:

  • The Learning Community: unlimited group coaching, weekly live sessions with Michael, Entrepreneur Success Managers, 5,000+ modules and a community of founders who understand exactly what you're carrying.
  • The free Dermer Diagnosis: scores five areas of your business so you can see which problems are driving the stress, with a 30-day plan to fix them.
  • The Founder Clarity Hour: a one-on-one hour with a senior consultant for the decision you've been carrying alone.
  • The Entrepreneur Survival Guide: a $25 playbook on resilience, finding your playground and using AI to take work off your plate.
  • The Founder Blueprint and Sidekick: for larger companies that need to redesign the CEO role so the business stops depending on one exhausted person.

The bottom line

Burnout isn't a badge. It's a signal that the business is asking more than one person can give. The data shows most founders are sacrificing sleep, pay, health and relationships, and most still believe in what they're building. The goal isn't to care less. It's to build a business, and a support system, that lets you keep going.

If you're feeling overwhelmed or unsafe, please reach out to a mental health professional or a local crisis line.

Frequently asked questions

paragraph.html:
"We're too small to be a target."

It's one of the most common things small business owners say about cybersecurity, and one of the most dangerous. The logic seems reasonable: why would criminals bother with a 15-person company when there are banks and hospitals to attack?

hive.html:
There's a moment many founders know too well. You've built a solid business. Customers are coming. Growth is right there. All you need is capital to hire, buy inventory or expand capacity. You apply for a loan, and the bank says: maybe, some of it, if you personally guarantee it.

Suddenly, the question isn't whether your business can grow. It's whether you're willing to put your house, savings and family security behind that growth.

This article looks at what the 2026 data says about small business funding and walks through seven alternatives that can help you grow without betting everything you own.

The funding reality in 2026

The Federal Reserve's 2026 Report on Employer Firms shows how common that path is.

  • 60% of small businesses applied for financing.
  • Of those that applied, only 42% got the full amount and 22% got nothing.
  • Among firms carrying debt, 59% used a personal guarantee, and 51% pledged business assets.

And the reasons founders are borrowing aren't always about growth.

It's worth remembering why so many founders are borrowing: 77% of employer firms named rising costs or tariffs as a financial challenge. Growth isn't the only driver; survival is too. Meanwhile, NFIB data shows only 25% of owners borrow regularly, compared with a historical average of 34%.

What a personal guarantee really means

A personal guarantee means that if the business can't repay, you will, from personal assets. For many founders, that includes their home equity, savings and sometimes their spouse's assets.

Personal guarantees aren't inherently wrong. They're often the price of access to capital for a young business. However, they turn a business risk into a family risk, and founders often sign them under time pressure without fully considering alternatives or negotiating terms.

Seven ways to fund growth without betting the house

1. Customer-funded growth. Deposits, prepayments, annual plans and retainers can fund growth with your customers' money. Many service businesses, software companies and manufacturers grow this way. Ask yourself: would your best customers pay upfront for a discount or priority?

2. Revenue-based financing. Some lenders advance capital in exchange for a percentage of future revenue until a fixed amount is repaid. Payments flex with revenue, and personal guarantees may be lighter or absent, though costs can be higher than bank loans. Read terms carefully.

3. Equipment financing. When the growth need is equipment, the equipment itself can serve as collateral. This can reduce or avoid the need for broader personal guarantees.

4. Invoice financing or factoring. If your capital need is caused by slow-paying customers, financing against receivables can unlock cash you've already earned. It costs money, but it's tied to the actual cause of the gap.

5. SBA-backed loans. SBA programs can offer longer terms and lower down payments. They typically still require personal guarantees from significant owners, but the structure and terms may be more manageable. Talk to an SBA-experienced lender.

6. Grants, competitions and community lenders. Community development financial institutions (CDFIs), local economic development programs, industry grants and pitch competitions can provide capital on favorable terms. They take time to find and apply for, but they don't come with equity dilution.

7. Small banks. In the Fed survey, small banks had the highest full-approval rate, at 57%. Relationships matter there; therefore, start one before you need it.

Negotiating the guarantee

If a guarantee is unavoidable, it may still be negotiable. Founders can ask for:

  • A limited guarantee, capped at a specific amount rather than the full loan.
  • A burn-off provision, where the guarantee reduces or ends after a period of on-time payments or when certain financial targets are met.
  • Exclusion of specific assets, such as a primary residence where possible.
  • Guarantees only from the principal owner, not every partner or spouse.

Lenders won't always agree. But many founders never ask, and some lenders have more flexibility than they advertise. Have a lawyer review any guarantee before you sign.

Questions to ask before taking any capital

  1. What exactly will this money do, and how quickly will it pay back?
  2. What happens if it pays back slower than planned? Can the business still make payments in a bad quarter?
  3. What am I personally risking, and is my family aware of it?
  4. Have I compared at least three options?
  5. Could I fund part of this from customers, operations or a smaller first step?
  6. Who outside the company has reviewed this decision?

A worked example

Consider a contract manufacturer with $3.2M in revenue that needs $400,000 for a new machine and working capital for a large new customer. The bank offers $250,000 with a full personal guarantee.

Instead of signing immediately, the founder finances the machine through equipment financing secured by the machine itself, negotiates a 25% deposit from the new customer to cover materials, and uses a smaller bank line of $100,000 with a guarantee capped at that amount and a burn-off after 18 months. The business gets the capital it needs. The founder's house is no longer the backstop for the whole plan.

Matching the money to the need

One of the most useful habits in funding is matching the type of capital to the type of need. Mismatches are where founders get hurt.

  • Short-term gaps caused by slow-paying customers are best addressed with tools tied to receivables, like invoice financing or a revolving line of credit, not long-term loans.
  • Equipment and physical assets are best funded with equipment financing or loans that match the asset's useful life.
  • Growth with uncertain payback, like a new market or product, is better funded with customer prepayments, operating cash or equity than with debt that has fixed monthly payments.
  • Ongoing operating losses are a warning sign. Borrowing to cover them without a clear plan to fix the underlying problem usually makes things worse.

Before choosing a lender, write down which category your need falls into. That single step eliminates many poor options.

Talk to your family before you sign

Founders often sign personal guarantees without fully discussing them at home, either to protect their partner from worry or because the decision feels urgent. That usually backfires. A guarantee affects the whole household. Explaining what's at stake, what the plan is and what happens if things go wrong builds trust and often leads to better decisions. Sometimes, saying it out loud is enough to realize the risk isn't worth it, or that a smaller step would work.

Why funding decisions feel so lonely

Funding decisions combine money, risk, family and the future of the business. They're often made quickly, under pressure, with lenders whose incentives aren't the same as yours. Many founders sign because they don't know what alternatives exist or don't have anyone to ask.

That's a solvable problem.

Where The Lonely Entrepreneur helps

The Lonely Entrepreneur helps founders make capital decisions with clarity and experienced input:

  • Access 400+ financing sources. The Learning Community includes more than 400 financing sources, 5,000+ learning modules, unlimited group coaching and weekly live sessions with Michael Dermer.
  • Check your lender-readiness. The free Dermer Diagnosis scores five areas of your business and highlights the exposures lenders are likely to see.
  • Pressure-test one big capital decision. A Founder Clarity Hour gives you 60 minutes with a senior consultant and a written plan with three dos and three don'ts.
  • Build the money plan from $1M to $5M. The Founder Blueprint covers customers, team, money, the CEO role and AI over five weeks.
  • Get a capital-strategy partner from $5M to $50M. Sidekick offers a senior partner for CEO-level issues with weekly check-ins.
  • Planning an exit? The Exit Sidekick provides an independent advisor for selling your company.

The bottom line

The bank saying "some of it" isn't the end of your growth plan. Customer funding, revenue-based financing, equipment financing, invoice financing, SBA loans, grants and small banks all offer paths forward. And when a guarantee is unavoidable, it's often negotiable. The key is to explore options before you sign, and to make the decision with people who've been there.

Frequently asked questions

How many small business loan applicants get the full amount? Only 42% of applicants did in the Federal Reserve's 2026 survey; 22% got nothing.

How common are personal guarantees? 59% of small firms with outstanding debt used a personal guarantee, and 51% pledged business assets.

What are alternatives to bank loans for small businesses? Customer prepayments and deposits, revenue-based financing, equipment financing, invoice financing, SBA-backed loans, grants and CDFIs, and small banks.

Can a personal guarantee be negotiated? Often, yes. Founders can ask for a capped guarantee, a burn-off provision or exclusion of specific assets. Have a lawyer review it.

Where can founders find financing sources and advice? The Lonely Entrepreneur's Learning Community includes 400+ financing sources, and its Founder Clarity Hour, Founder Blueprint and Sidekick programs help founders make capital decisions.

  • NFIB Small Business Economic Trends, October 2026
  • The Lonely Entrepreneur

Dear founder,

You haven't told anyone yet.

Not your team, because they need you steady. Not your spouse, at least not all of it, because they already worry. Not your friends, because they'd say "you'll figure it out" and then change the subject. So you carry it: the cash that's tighter than it looks, the customer who might leave, the partner who stopped pulling their weight, the number you check three times a day.

I want to say a few things you may not be hearing from anyone else. And because you're the kind of person who trusts numbers more than reassurance, I'll show you some of those, too.

You are far from the only one

It can feel like every other founder is doing fine. Their posts are full of wins, launches and hiring announcements. Yours would be, too, if you posted. But here's what founders say when someone asks them privately.

In Bluevine's 2026 survey of 781 owners, 68% lose at least one full night of sleep a month over money, 62% reduced or skipped their own pay in the past year and 53% felt emotionally drained by financial stress. In YouGov's research for the Start Up Loans Company, 55% of owners wish they had someone to turn to.

So when you sit in your car for ten minutes before walking into the office, composing your face, you're not alone. You're in the majority. It's just a quiet majority.

First, this is normal

Not easy, but normal. Almost every business that has lasted went through a stretch exactly like this. The founders you admire had months when they couldn't sleep either; they just didn't post about it.

That doesn't make it smaller. It means it's survivable, and that there are people who've found their way through it.

Second, keeping it secret makes it heavier

Silence feels like protection. In reality, it removes every source of help. Problems that look impossible at 2 a.m. often look solvable after one honest conversation with someone who's been there.

There's also a practical cost. Decisions made in isolation tend to be delayed, distorted or hidden. Bluevine found 68% of owners delayed or avoided a major business decision in the past year because of financial stress. The longer a hard decision waits, the more expensive it usually becomes.

Third, being "the strong one" is a role, not a requirement

Your team doesn't need you to be fearless. Instead, they need you to be honest enough to lead and steady enough to decide. You can be both while admitting you're not sure.

In fact, teams often handle the truth better than founders expect. "We had a hard quarter. Here's what we're doing about it, and here's what I need from you" builds more trust than a forced smile and a sudden round of cuts nobody saw coming.

Fourth, the decision you're avoiding is probably the one that matters

Usually there is one: a conversation, a cut, a price, a person. Avoiding it costs more every week. Making it, even imperfectly, gives you back the energy that avoidance is eating.

Try this. Write it down in one sentence. Then write what waiting is costing you each week, in money, energy or trust. Then write what information you're actually missing. If the answer to the last one is "nothing," the decision isn't blocked by information. It's blocked by discomfort. And discomfort is something people can help you carry.

Finally, you are more than this company

Your worth isn't the revenue line. If the business struggles, you haven't failed as a person; you're doing something genuinely hard.

It's easy to forget that when the business is your name, your savings and most of your waking hours. But the person who started this company had value before it existed and will have value whatever happens to it. Hold on to that person. They're going to need to make some good decisions soon, and they'll make them better if they're not also carrying shame.

What telling someone actually does

YouGov's research found that 59% of owners feel more connected when they know other leaders share their experiences, and 74% say running their business has made them more resilient. Yet only 38% actively connect with other business leaders.

That gap, between how much founders benefit from connection and how few seek it, is where a lot of unnecessary suffering lives.

When you tell the right person, a few things happen. The problem gets smaller because it's out of your head and on the table. You hear that someone else survived something similar. You get one or two practical ideas you hadn't considered. And, often most importantly, you sleep a little better that night.

  • Has run a business, so they understand the weight without needing it explained.
  • Has nothing to sell you, so their advice isn't tilted.
  • Will tell you the truth, even when it's uncomfortable.
  • Will keep it confidential.
  • Will ask questions before giving answers.

  • "I'm stuck on a decision and I don't trust my own judgment on it right now. Can I walk you through it?"
  • "Things are harder than they look from the outside. I don't need you to fix it. I just need to say it."

Here's what I'd ask of you. Write down, in one sentence, what's actually wrong. Then tell one person who has run a business. Not to fix it; just to say it out loud.

If you don't have that person, find a room of them.

  • The Learning Community is a community of founders you can be honest with, who have lived it and have nothing to sell you. It includes unlimited group coaching, weekly live sessions with Michael, Entrepreneur Success Managers and 5,000+ learning modules.
  • A Founder Clarity Hour is a private, one-on-one hour with a senior consultant for the decision you've been avoiding. You leave with a written plan.
  • The free Dermer Diagnosis helps you see, in about eight minutes, which areas of the business are driving the pressure, with a 30-day action plan.
  • The Entrepreneur Survival Guide is a $25 playbook on resilience and surviving the hard stretches.

You built something from nothing. That took courage. Asking for help takes the same kind.

With respect, The Lonely Entrepreneur

If you're feeling overwhelmed or unsafe, please reach out to a mental health professional or a local crisis line.

Frequently asked questions

Is it normal for founders to hide business problems? Yes. Many founders hide stress from their teams, families and friends. 55% of owners say they wish they had someone to turn to, per YouGov research for the Start Up Loans Company.

How many business owners lose sleep over money? 68% lose at least one full night of sleep a month due to financial worries, according to Bluevine's 2026 research.

Why does keeping business problems secret make them worse? Isolation removes outside input, which leads to delayed and distorted decisions. Bluevine found 68% of owners delayed or avoided a major decision because of financial stress.

Who should a founder talk to about business struggles? Someone who has run a business, has nothing to sell, will tell the truth and will keep it confidential, such as an experienced founder or a structured founder community.

Where can founders find a confidential peer community? The Lonely Entrepreneur's Learning Community offers group coaching, weekly sessions with Michael Dermer and a community of founders at similar stages.

telegraph.html:
Most founders don't have a decision problem. Instead, they have a decision backlog: dozens of choices made on the fly, a few big ones postponed for months, and no time set aside to look at either.

That backlog is more common, and more expensive, than most owners realize. This article shares the data behind it and a simple ritual that fixes it in 30 minutes a week. No software needed; a notebook works.

The decision backlog, by the numbers

Bluevine's 2026 survey of 781 small business owners found something striking.

  • 68% delayed or avoided a major business decision in the past 12 months because of financial stress: hiring, buying equipment, expanding.
  • 71% report moderate to extremely high financial stress.
  • 9% delayed big decisions repeatedly or on a regular basis.

In other words, two out of three owners have at least one important decision sitting in limbo. And Patriot Software's 2026 research shows the toll that takes: 53.5% of owners lose sleep over their business at least a few times a week.

Undecided decisions don't stay quiet. They replay at night, drain energy during the day and quietly cost money while they wait.

Why founders postpone decisions

It's rarely laziness. Usually, it's one of these:

  • Fear of being wrong in front of the team, investors or family.
  • Missing information, or the belief that more information will make the choice easier.
  • No one to talk it through with, so the decision loops in one head.
  • No deadline, so there's always a reason to wait until next week.
  • Too many small decisions, crowding out the big ones.

The ritual below addresses each of these directly.

The ritual at a glance

Pick a fixed slot, ideally Friday afternoon when the week is still fresh. Close email. Set a timer. The ritual has four parts: review, name, date and stop.

Part 1: Review last week's calls (10 minutes)

List the five most important decisions you made this week. For each, write one line:

  • What did I decide?
  • What did I expect to happen?
  • What actually happened so far?

The point isn't to judge yourself. Rather, it's to notice patterns. Over a few weeks you'll see them: you hire too fast, you discount too easily, you say yes to customers you should decline.

This is also how founders get better at deciding. Without a record, every decision feels new. With one, you build a personal database of what works for you.

Part 2: Name the decision you're avoiding (5 minutes)

Every founder has one. A conversation with a partner, a price increase, a person who isn't working out, a lease, a loan.

Write it down in one sentence. Then answer two questions:

  • What is waiting costing me each week?
  • What information am I actually missing?

Frequently, the honest answer to the second question is "nothing." In that case, the decision isn't blocked by information; it's blocked by discomfort.

If you're not missing any information, the decision isn't blocked by information. It's blocked by discomfort.

Naming that is powerful. Discomfort can be managed: by talking to someone, by shrinking the decision or by setting a date.

Part 3: Set decision dates (10 minutes)

For each open decision, assign:

  • A decision date. When you'll decide regardless.
  • The smallest reversible version. Can you test it instead of committing fully?
  • One outside opinion. Who has faced this before and could pressure-test it?

Consequently, open loops become scheduled decisions, and your mind stops replaying them at night.

The "smallest reversible version" is especially useful. Instead of "hire a salesperson," try "hire a contractor for 90 days." Instead of "raise all prices," try "raise prices for new customers this month." Reversible tests turn scary decisions into experiments.

Part 4: Choose one thing to stop (5 minutes)

Founders add tasks constantly but rarely remove any. Therefore, end the review by choosing one recurring thing to stop, delegate or automate next week.

Over a year, that's 50 things off your plate. That's how founders create time for the decisions that matter.

Why this works

Decisions made alone tend to be delayed, distorted or hidden. This ritual counters all three: it puts deadlines on delay, adds outside input to distortion, and makes your reasoning visible, even if only to yourself.

It also works because it's small. Thirty minutes is easy to protect. And because it happens every week, nothing important sits for more than seven days without being looked at.

A worked example

Here's what a real Friday review might look like for the owner of a 12-person marketing agency.

Part 1, last week's calls: Agreed to a 15% discount for a new client (expected: win the deal; actual: won it, but scope is already creeping). Hired a freelance designer (expected: faster turnaround; actual: too early to tell). Declined a speaking event (expected: more time; actual: used the time on proposals). The pattern after a few weeks: discounts keep leading to scope creep.

Part 2, the avoided decision: "Should we let go of our longest-standing client, who's now unprofitable?" Cost of waiting: about $3,000 a month in unbilled hours and a frustrated team. Missing information: honestly, none.

Part 3, decision dates: Decide by the end of the month. Smallest reversible version: propose a repriced scope first and let the client choose. Outside opinion: ask two agency founders in the peer group who've repriced legacy clients.

Part 4, one thing to stop: Stop attending the weekly status call for a client the account manager already handles.

Thirty minutes. One avoided decision now has a date, a test and two advisors. One recurring task is gone. Multiply that by 52 weeks.

Common mistakes with the ritual

  • Turning it into a to-do list review. This is about decisions, not tasks.
  • Skipping Part 2 when it's uncomfortable. That's precisely when it matters most.
  • Setting dates and ignoring them. If a date passes, the next review should ask why.
  • Doing it only when things are bad. The habit is most valuable when it's consistent.

Making it stick

A few tips from founders who've kept this habit for months:

  • Put it in the calendar as a recurring meeting with yourself, and treat it like a client meeting.
  • Use the same notebook or document every week, so you can look back.
  • Start small. If 30 minutes feels like too much, do 15 and grow from there.
  • Review monthly. Once a month, read your last four reviews. Patterns jump out.
  • Do it with someone. A peer founder, a coach or a group makes it far more effective.

Even better: do Part 3 with other founders

The outside opinion in Part 3 is where most founders get stuck. It's easy to say "ask someone who's faced this." It's harder to actually have that person available on a Friday afternoon.

That's one reason The Lonely Entrepreneur runs weekly group coaching in its Learning Community: founders bring their avoided decisions and leave with dates and second opinions. The community includes unlimited group coaching, weekly live sessions with Michael Dermer, 5,000+ learning modules and tools and templates for exactly these kinds of decisions.

Other ways TLE helps:

  • One big decision you can't shake? Book a Founder Clarity Hour: 60 minutes with a senior consultant, a pre-call intake and a written action plan with three dos and three don'ts.
  • Not sure which area of your business needs the most decisions right now? The free Dermer Diagnosis scores five areas in about eight minutes.
  • Running a $1M to $5M business? The Founder Blueprint is a five-week program covering customers, team, money, the CEO role and AI.

- **68% delayed or avoided a major business decision** in the past 12 months because of financial stress: hiring, buying equipment, expanding.
- **71%** report moderate to extremely high financial stress.
- **9%** delayed big decisions repeatedly or on a regular basis.

In other words, two out of three owners have at least one important decision sitting in limbo. And Patriot Software's 2026 research shows the toll that takes: **53.5% of owners lose sleep over their business at least a few times a week.**

Undecided decisions don't stay quiet. They replay at night, drain energy during the day and quietly cost money while they wait.

## Why founders postpone decisions

It's rarely laziness. Usually, it's one of these:

- **Fear of being wrong** in front of the team, investors or family.
- **Missing information,** or the belief that more information will make the choice easier.
- **No one to talk it through with,** so the decision loops in one head.
- **No deadline,** so there's always a reason to wait until next week.
- **Too many small decisions,** crowding out the big ones.

The ritual below addresses each of these directly.

Pick a fixed slot, ideally Friday afternoon when the week is still fresh. Close email. Set a timer. The ritual has four parts: review, name, date and stop.

## Part 1: Review last week's calls (10 minutes)

List the five most important decisions you made this week. For each, write one line:

- **What did I decide?**
- **What did I expect to happen?**
- **What actually happened so far?**

The point isn't to judge yourself. Rather, it's to notice patterns. Over a few weeks you'll see them: you hire too fast, you discount too easily, you say yes to customers you should decline.

This is also how founders get better at deciding. Without a record, every decision feels new. With one, you build a personal database of what works for you.

## Part 2: Name the decision you're avoiding (5 minutes)

Every founder has one. A conversation with a partner, a price increase, a person who isn't working out, a lease, a loan.

Write it down in one sentence. Then answer two questions:

- **What is waiting costing me each week?**
- **What information am I actually missing?**

Frequently, the honest answer to the second question is "nothing." In that case, the decision isn't blocked by information; it's blocked by discomfort.

Naming that is powerful. Discomfort can be managed: by talking to someone, by shrinking the decision or by setting a date.

## Part 3: Set decision dates (10 minutes)

For each open decision, assign:

- **A decision date.** When you'll decide regardless.
- **The smallest reversible version.** Can you test it instead of committing fully?
- **One outside opinion.** Who has faced this before and could pressure-test it?

Consequently, open loops become scheduled decisions, and your mind stops replaying them at night.

The "smallest reversible version" is especially useful. Instead of "hire a salesperson," try "hire a contractor for 90 days." Instead of "raise all prices," try "raise prices for new customers this month." Reversible tests turn scary decisions into experiments.

## Part 4: Choose one thing to stop (5 minutes)

Founders add tasks constantly but rarely remove any. Therefore, end the review by choosing one recurring thing to stop, delegate or automate next week.

Over a year, that's 50 things off your plate. That's how founders create time for the decisions that matter.

Most founders know they should delegate more. However, "delegate more" is advice, not a method. Here's a method based on simple arithmetic, and the data on why it matters more in 2026 than ever.

The admin load is real

Before the math, it's worth seeing what founders are carrying. Bluevine's 2026 survey of 781 small business owners asked about their top financial stressors.

Cash flow timing (41%) and paying monthly bills (39%) top the list, followed by quarterly and annual taxes (25%), bookkeeping and expenses (22%) and making payroll (20%).

Notice how much of that list is administrative work that someone else could do, or at least prepare. Meanwhile, Patriot Software's 2026 survey found 84.4% of owners have sacrificed health, relationships or wellbeing for the business, and 45.8% have given up family time.

Those two facts are connected. Founders who never hand off the admin pay for it with the hours they'd otherwise spend on growth, rest or people they love.

Step 1: Find your real hourly value

Start with a number you'd rather not calculate.

Take what you want the business to earn you in a year, including profit you'd reinvest. Divide by the hours you actually work. For example, if you want $200,000 and you work 2,500 hours, your target value is $80 per hour.

Now here's the uncomfortable part: the work that grows the business, like selling, key relationships, pricing and hiring, is usually worth far more than that. Meanwhile, much of your week is spent on tasks you could hire out for $20 to $40 an hour.

Step 2: Log one normal week

For five days, write down what you do in 30-minute blocks. Don't change your behavior; just record it.

Then label each block:

  • A: Only I can do this (strategy, key clients, final hiring calls).
  • B: Someone else could do it with training.
  • C: Someone else could do it today (scheduling, data entry, basic bookkeeping, routine customer emails).

Most founders are shocked by how much of the week is B and C. It's common to find that half the week, or more, is work someone else could do.

Step 3: Price the handoff

For each C task, multiply the hours per week by the market rate to outsource it. Then compare that with what those hours are worth if you spend them on A work.

For instance: 8 hours a week of admin, outsourced at $30 an hour, costs $240. If those 8 hours go into sales or a key client, even one extra deal a month usually covers it many times over.

The math isn't only about revenue. Those 8 hours could also be evenings with your family, sleep or exercise, all of which make you a better decision-maker. That's a return, too.

Step 4: Start with the most annoying, not the most important

Founders often try to delegate something big first, and it goes badly. Instead, start with a C task that drains you most. It's low risk, it frees energy immediately, and it builds your confidence in handing things off.

Good first handoffs include inbox triage, calendar management, invoicing and payment reminders, data entry, travel booking, social media scheduling and basic bookkeeping.

Step 5: Write the "how" once

Before you hand anything over, record a short screen video or write a one-page checklist. As a result, the task becomes transferable, and the next handoff is faster.

A simple format works:

  1. What the task is and why it matters.
  2. When it happens (daily, weekly, triggered by an event).
  3. Step-by-step instructions with screenshots or a short video.
  4. What "done well" looks like.
  5. When to escalate to you.

Store these in one shared place. Over time, you'll build an operations manual without ever sitting down to write one.

Step 6: Move B tasks next

Once C tasks are off your plate, look at B: work someone could do with training. This takes more investment, but it's where real leverage comes from. Pick one B task per quarter, train someone properly and give them ownership, not just instructions.

Where AI fits in

In 2026, delegation doesn't always mean a person. AI tools can now draft routine emails, summarize documents, categorize expenses, prepare first drafts of reports and handle parts of customer support. The same math applies: if a tool removes hours of C work for a modest monthly cost, it's likely worth it. The key is to start with a specific, repetitive task, not a vague hope that AI will "make things faster."

A sample week, before and after

Consider the owner of a $900K home services company who logged a normal week. Of 55 hours, 14 were C work: scheduling, invoicing, chasing payments, ordering supplies and answering routine customer emails. Another 12 were B work: quoting standard jobs and training new technicians on procedures that could be documented.

After handing off the C work to a part-time operations assistant at $25 an hour (about $350 a week) and recording procedures for quoting, the owner freed up roughly 20 hours a week within two months. Ten went into calling past customers and commercial property managers, which produced two recurring maintenance contracts. The rest went into, in the owner's words, "having dinner with my kids again."

That's delegation math in practice: a modest weekly cost, a measurable revenue return and a return you can't put on a spreadsheet.

How to choose who to delegate to

For C tasks, a part-time assistant, a virtual assistant or a specialized service (bookkeeping, payroll) usually works best. For B tasks, look inside your team first: who has shown initiative, asks good questions and wants more responsibility? Delegating to an existing team member is also a growth opportunity for them, which helps retention.

Why founders don't delegate

The math is usually clear. The obstacles are emotional: "It's faster if I do it." "Nobody does it like me." "I can't afford help yet." Each is partly true in the short term and wrong over a year.

"It's faster if I do it" is true once. It's false on the tenth time.

"Nobody does it like me" is often true. But "good enough, done by someone else" frees you for work only you can do.

"I can't afford help" deserves a real calculation. If your hour is worth $80 and help costs $30, you often can't afford not to.

There's also a deeper reason: control. For many founders, doing everything themselves feels safer. Letting go means trusting others with something you built. That's a real emotional hurdle, and it's easier to clear with people who've done it.

Common delegation mistakes

  • Delegating without context. People need to know why a task matters, not just how to do it.
  • Abdicating instead of delegating. Handing something off and never checking in leads to surprises.
  • Taking it back at the first mistake. Expect a learning curve. Coach, don't reclaim.
  • Delegating tasks but not decisions. Real leverage comes when people own outcomes.

  • Get a CEO-level partner. For $5M to $50M companies, Sidekick helps leaders step fully into the CEO role.

Try it this week: log five days, label every block A, B or C, and hand off one C task by next Friday.

Not because they lack access. Most small business owners have an accountant, a banker, an insurance broker, maybe a lawyer and a consultant or two. Rather, the problem is subtler: many of those people are paid in ways that don't line up with the founder's interests. And over time, founders notice.

What founders say about support

The 2026 data paints a picture of owners who feel surprisingly alone, despite being surrounded by professionals.

  • 58% of owners feel the system, meaning government, financial institutions and the economy, is mostly or completely stacked against them (Patriot Software, 2026).
  • 27.6% of veteran owners with five or more years in business feel "completely unsupported."
  • 55% wish they had someone to turn to for support (YouGov for the Start Up Loans Company).
  • Yet 59% feel more connected when they know other leaders share their experiences.

That last pair is telling. Founders want support. They benefit enormously when they find people who understand. But many don't trust the people around them enough to be honest.

The incentive problem

Consider who usually gives small business owners advice:

  • Bankers, who are rewarded for lending.
  • Brokers, often paid commissions on what they sell.
  • Consultants, paid for more hours or bigger projects.
  • Software vendors, who want you on their platform.
  • Online gurus, who sell courses about the advice.

None of these people are necessarily acting in bad faith. Many are excellent and genuinely care. Still, each one has an incentive that can tilt the advice. Consequently, founders learn to discount what they hear, and many end up trusting no one.

That's the trust trap: plenty of expertise, very little alignment.

How the trust trap hurts the business

When founders stop trusting advice, three things tend to happen.

They make decisions alone. Without trusted input, important calls get made in isolation, which leads to delays and blind spots.

They over-rely on one voice. Some founders swing the other way and trust one advisor completely, often the most confident one, without checking incentives.

They learn the expensive way. Without honest advice, founders repeat mistakes others could have warned them about: the wrong hire, the bad lease, the loan that should have been smaller.

How to tell aligned advice from sales

A few practical tests help separate them.

1. Ask how they get paid. Directly and early. Good advisors answer clearly. Vague answers are a signal.

2. Notice whether they ever say "don't." Someone who never recommends doing less, spending less or waiting is probably selling.

3. Check whether their advice changes when your budget does. Aligned advice is about your outcome, not the size of the engagement.

4. Look for people who have made the decision themselves. An operator who has hired, borrowed, priced and fired will see risks that a theorist misses.

5. Get a second opinion before irreversible decisions. Not ten opinions; two good ones.

6. Watch what happens when you push back. Trustworthy advisors welcome questions. Defensive ones are protecting something.

7. Look at their track record with people like you. Ask for references from businesses your size and stage, not just their biggest names.

Who to trust instead

The most reliable source of honest advice is often the least formal: other founders who have faced the same decisions and have nothing to sell you.

They have no commission on your loan, no stake in your software choice, and no reason to flatter you. Moreover, they remember exactly how the mistake felt, which makes them unusually direct.

The challenge is finding them. Founder friends are scattered, busy and rarely in your industry. As a result, the conversations happen too late, if at all.

Build your circle on purpose

Here's a simple structure:

  • One operator mentor who's a few years ahead of you.
  • Three to five peer founders at a similar stage, ideally in different industries.
  • Paid professionals for execution (legal, tax, accounting), chosen with the incentive questions above.

Then meet regularly, not just in a crisis.

Different industries matter more than founders expect. Peers in your own industry may be competitors or share the same blind spots. A restaurant owner, a software founder and a contractor often see each other's problems more clearly than people in the same field.

What a trusted circle looks like in practice

Imagine you're deciding whether to sign a five-year lease for a larger space. Your broker says it's a great deal; they're paid on the lease. Your banker says you qualify for the build-out loan; they're paid on the loan. Your team is excited about the new space.

Now imagine bringing the same decision to three founders who've signed leases before. One asks about your cash runway if revenue dips 20%. Another shares how a personal guarantee on a lease nearly cost them their house. The third suggests negotiating a shorter initial term with an option to extend. Same decision, very different quality of thinking, because nobody in that second conversation earns anything from your answer.

Red flags in an advisor

Beyond incentives, some behaviors signal that an advisor may not be right for you:

  • Certainty about everything. Real experts acknowledge uncertainty and trade-offs.
  • Pressure to decide quickly, especially when the decision benefits them.
  • Generic advice that could apply to any business.
  • Reluctance to put recommendations in writing.
  • No interest in your numbers, goals or constraints before giving answers.
  • Disparaging every alternative rather than explaining trade-offs.

None of these mean someone is dishonest. But they're signals to slow down and get another view.

Questions to ask any new advisor

Before you engage a new accountant, consultant, broker or coach, ask these five questions. Their answers, and how comfortable they are answering, tell you a lot.

  1. "How exactly are you paid for this work, and do you earn anything from what you recommend?"
  2. "When have you advised a client not to do something that would have earned you more?"
  3. "What kinds of businesses do you work best with, and which don't you take on?"
  4. "Can I speak with two clients at my stage?"
  5. "What would make you tell me you're not the right fit?"

Trust is built, not found

The founders with the strongest circles didn't stumble into them. They invested over time: showing up consistently, sharing honestly, helping others and following through. Trust grows when people see each other's real decisions and real outcomes over months and years.

That's why one-off networking events rarely create a trusted circle. Regular, structured contact with the same small group of people does. If you want honest advice when it matters most, start building those relationships when you don't urgently need them.

Why it's worth paying for a trusted room

Some founders resist paying for peer communities or coaching because it feels like another vendor. That's fair, and the same incentive tests apply. The difference is what you're paying for: access to people whose only job is to help you make a better decision, with no stake in which decision you make.

Where to find that room

That's the whole idea behind The Lonely Entrepreneur. Founder Michael Dermer built a company to 1,000 employees and learned firsthand how hard it is to find unconflicted advice. TLE has since helped more than 500,000 founders.

  • The Learning Community gives you a room of founders who've lived it and have nothing to sell, with unlimited group coaching, weekly live sessions with Michael and 5,000+ learning modules.
  • Our Entrepreneur Trust Index looks at who founders can really rely on.
  • A Founder Clarity Hour offers one-on-one time with a senior consultant on a specific decision.
  • The Founder Blueprint helps $1M to $5M founders build a plan with five hours of one-on-one coaching.
  • Sidekick pairs $5M to $50M CEOs with a senior partner who's been in the seat; TLE has supported 600+ CEOs this way.
  • Selling the business? The Exit Sidekick offers an independent advisor, not a broker paid on the deal.

Read more: The Founder Overwhelm Trap, on why founders lose sleep, skip their own paycheck and drown in decisions.

Frequently asked questions

How many owners feel unsupported? 58% feel the system is stacked against them, and 27.6% of veteran owners feel completely unsupported, according to Patriot Software's 2026 survey.

How can I tell if advice is aligned? Ask how they're paid, notice whether they ever say "don't," check whether the advice changes with your budget and look for people who have made the decision themselves.

Who gives founders the most honest advice? Other founders who have faced the same decisions and have nothing to sell.

Where can founders find a trusted peer circle? The Lonely Entrepreneur's Learning Community, Founder Blueprint and Sidekick programs connect founders with experienced peers and senior partners.

  • YouGov for the Start Up Loans Company: almost half of UK smaller business leaders feel isolated
  • The Lonely Entrepreneur
