steemit.title: Laid Off in 2026 and Thinking of Starting Something? 7 Decisions for Your First 90 Days
steemit.subtitle: Americans started 5.5 million businesses in 2025. Here's a practical roadmap for turning a layoff into a business, without burning through your savings.
steemit.html:
A layoff can feel like the end of something. For a growing number of people, however, it's the start of a company.

Americans started more than 5.5 million new businesses in 2025, according to the US Census Bureau. Many were founded by people who'd just lost a job, saw AI reshaping their industry or decided they'd rather bet on themselves than on the next employer.

If you're weighing that move, the first 90 days matter more than the idea. This guide covers what the data says about the first year and the seven decisions that tend to shape everything after.

The first year, by the numbers

Starting a business is exciting. The data also shows it's hard, especially at the beginning.

  • 58.8% of new owners have skipped or delayed their own paycheck (Patriot Software, 2026).
  • 65% of owners in their first year report feeling lonely (YouGov for the Start Up Loans Company).

  • 37.7% of new owners have delayed or gone without health insurance because of business costs, compared with 24.6% of all owners.
  • 29.6% of new owners lose sleep almost every night, compared with 12.7% of veteran owners.

None of this is a reason not to start. It's a reason to start with a plan. The founders who make it through year one tend to make a few key decisions early and deliberately.

Decision 1: Decide your runway before your business

Before you register a company, calculate how many months you can live without income: savings, severance and any partner income, minus essential monthly costs. That number sets the pace of every other decision.

As a rule of thumb, decide in advance what you'll do if you reach a certain point, for example six months left, without paying customers. Having that rule makes the journey far less frightening.

Don't forget health insurance in the calculation. As the data shows, it's one of the first things new owners cut, and one of the riskiest.

Decision 2: Start from a problem you've seen up close

The strongest early businesses usually come from a problem the founder has already watched someone pay to solve. Your previous job is a goldmine here: which tasks did your company outsource, struggle with, or complain about?

Ask yourself:

  • What did my old employer pay vendors or consultants for?
  • What problems did customers complain about that nobody fixed?
  • What do people in my industry consistently ask me for help with?

Your industry knowledge and network are your biggest unfair advantages. Use them.

Decision 3: Sell before you build

Talk to 20 potential customers before investing serious money. Ask about the problem, not your idea. Then try to get a commitment, whether a deposit, a pilot or a letter of intent. In other words, let customers fund your proof.

Good questions to ask:

  • "How do you handle this today?"
  • "What does it cost you, in time or money?"
  • "What have you tried that didn't work?"
  • "If I could solve this, what would that be worth to you?"

If people won't commit even a small amount, that's valuable information, and it's much cheaper to learn now than after building.

Decision 4: Choose a business model with early cash

Services, consulting and productized offers can generate revenue in weeks. By contrast, software products or inventory-heavy businesses often take months. Consequently, many successful founders start with a service and turn it into a product later.

A productized service, meaning a clearly defined offer with a fixed scope and price, is often the sweet spot: faster to sell than custom consulting and faster to launch than software.

Decision 5: Keep fixed costs near zero

No office, no long contracts, no big software stack. Every fixed cost shortens your runway. Use free tiers and month-to-month tools until revenue justifies more.

This is also where AI helps first-time founders in 2026. Tasks that once required hires or agencies, like drafting marketing copy, building a simple website, organizing bookkeeping or answering routine customer questions, can often be handled with inexpensive tools while you're small.

Decision 6: Set up the basics properly

A simple legal entity, a separate bank account, basic bookkeeping and clear contracts. These feel boring; nevertheless, fixing them later costs far more than doing them now.

Also set up:

  • A simple pricing sheet so you're not reinventing prices for every customer.
  • A standard agreement with payment terms, ideally with a deposit.
  • A weekly money check: cash in the bank, invoices outstanding, runway remaining.

Pay yourself something as soon as you can, even if it's small. It forces you to see the real economics of the business.

Decision 7: Don't do it alone

This is the decision people skip. Going from employee to founder means losing your manager, your colleagues and your feedback loop overnight. Moreover, you'll face decisions about pricing, clients and money with nobody to check your thinking.

The data backs this up: 65% of first-year owners feel lonely. Isolation leads to slower, worse decisions at exactly the moment when every decision matters most.

Find a group of founders early, people who've made the jump and will tell you the truth.

A simple 90-day plan

Days 1–30: Calculate runway. Write down your stop rule. List problems you've seen up close. Talk to 20 potential customers.

Days 31–60: Choose one offer with early cash. Set up the entity, bank account and contract. Get your first paying customer or signed pilot.

Days 61–90: Deliver well. Ask for referrals and testimonials. Decide, based on real results, whether to continue, adjust or stop.

Mistakes that cost new founders the most

Based on what experienced founders consistently say they'd do differently:

  • Spending months building before talking to customers. The market rarely wants exactly what you imagined.
  • Underpricing to win the first clients. Low prices are hard to raise later and attract the most demanding customers.
  • Saying yes to every opportunity. Early focus on one clear offer beats a scattered menu.
  • Mixing personal and business money. It makes taxes, decisions and stress worse.
  • Ignoring the stop rule. Founders who set a runway limit and then keep extending it often lose far more than they planned.
  • Hiding struggles from family. The people affected by your runway deserve to know where things stand.

What to do if the 90 days don't go to plan

Not every first attempt works, and that's normal. If you reach day 90 without paying customers, look honestly at what you learned. Was the problem real but your offer wrong? Was the price the issue? The audience? Many successful founders pivoted after their first 90 days, using exactly what they learned. Others went back to employment with new skills and a clearer idea for later. Both are legitimate outcomes. The only bad outcome is draining your savings while avoiding the question.

Where to go next

The Lonely Entrepreneur has a full guide for people in exactly this situation: Laid off in 2026? Read this before your next job search. When you're ready, there are several ways TLE helps new founders:

  • Find your playground. The Playground Report analyzes market saturation, white space, competitors, economics and risks, so you choose a market with room to win.
  • Get the survival playbook. The Entrepreneur Survival Guide ($25) covers finding your playground, brand chemistry, resilience and using AI as a tool.
  • Check your foundations. The free Dermer Diagnosis scores five areas of a business and gives you a 30-day plan.
  • Talk through the jump. A Founder Clarity Hour gives you 60 minutes with a senior consultant on your biggest decision.
  • Join a room of founders. The Learning Community offers group coaching, 5,000+ learning modules, 400+ financing sources and a founder community, with a 30-day free trial.

A layoff takes away a job. It doesn't take away what you know. Used well, those first 90 days can turn that knowledge into something that's yours.

Frequently asked questions

Should I start a business after a layoff? It can work well if you set your runway first, start from a problem you've seen up close and sell before you build.

How many new businesses were started in 2025? More than 5.5 million in the US, according to the US Census Bureau.

What business models generate cash fastest? Services, consulting and productized offers often generate revenue within weeks.

What's the biggest mistake new founders make after a layoff? Going it alone; 65% of first-year owners report feeling lonely, and losing a manager and colleagues removes your feedback loop overnight.

Where can new founders get support? The Lonely Entrepreneur offers a Playground Report, the Entrepreneur Survival Guide, a free Dermer Diagnosis, Founder Clarity Hours and a Learning Community with a 30-day free trial.

Sources

  • Patriot Software small business owner burnout survey 2026 (includes US Census Bureau figure)
  • YouGov for the Start Up Loans Company: almost half of UK smaller business leaders feel isolated
  • The Lonely Entrepreneur

A simple legal entity, a separate bank account, basic bookkeeping and clear contracts. These feel boring; nevertheless, fixing them later costs far more than doing them now.

Also set up:

- **A simple pricing sheet** so you're not reinventing prices for every customer.
- **A standard agreement** with payment terms, ideally with a deposit.
- **A weekly money check:** cash in the bank, invoices outstanding, runway remaining.

Pay yourself something as soon as you can, even if it's small. It forces you to see the real economics of the business.

## Decision 7: Don't do it alone

This is the decision people skip. Going from employee to founder means losing your manager, your colleagues and your feedback loop overnight. Moreover, you'll face decisions about pricing, clients and money with nobody to check your thinking.

The data backs this up: 65% of first-year owners feel lonely. Isolation leads to slower, worse decisions at exactly the moment when every decision matters most.

Find a group of founders early, people who've made the jump and will tell you the truth.

## A simple 90-day plan

**Days 1–30:** Calculate runway. Write down your stop rule. List problems you've seen up close. Talk to 20 potential customers.

**Days 31–60:** Choose one offer with early cash. Set up the entity, bank account and contract. Get your first paying customer or signed pilot.

**Days 61–90:** Deliver well. Ask for referrals and testimonials. Decide, based on real results, whether to continue, adjust or stop.

## Mistakes that cost new founders the most

Based on what experienced founders consistently say they'd do differently:

- **Spending months building before talking to customers.** The market rarely wants exactly what you imagined.
- **Underpricing to win the first clients.** Low prices are hard to raise later and attract the most demanding customers.
- **Saying yes to every opportunity.** Early focus on one clear offer beats a scattered menu.
- **Mixing personal and business money.** It makes taxes, decisions and stress worse.
- **Ignoring the stop rule.** Founders who set a runway limit and then keep extending it often lose far more than they planned.
- **Hiding struggles from family.** The people affected by your runway deserve to know where things stand.

## What to do if the 90 days don't go to plan

Not every first attempt works, and that's normal. If you reach day 90 without paying customers, look honestly at what you learned. Was the problem real but your offer wrong? Was the price the issue? The audience? Many successful founders pivoted after their first 90 days, using exactly what they learned. Others went back to employment with new skills and a clearer idea for later. Both are legitimate outcomes. The only bad outcome is draining your savings while avoiding the question.
